questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Edwin B. Flippo's classic definition of HRM lists six operative functions. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The six operative functions in this definition are procurement, development, compensation, integration, maintenance and separation of human resources. Advertising is a marketing activity, not an HR operative function. Options A, C and D are all part of the six-function list, from bringing people in (procurement) to their exit (separation).

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which definition presents HRM as 'a strategic approach to the management of an organization's most valued assets, the people working there'?
questions.explanation: This wording frames people as the organisation's most valued assets and treats HRM as strategic, which is the hallmark of Michael Armstrong's definition. Option C is the very short definition that HRM is the utilisation of individuals to achieve organisational objectives. Options A and D are earlier, more administrative definitions built around activities such as recruitment, procurement and compensation.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Taken as a whole, how did definitions of HRM change between the 1960s and the 2000s?

options.a: They moved from a strategic view of people to a purely payroll and record-keeping view
options.b: They remained essentially unchanged, describing HRM only as hiring and firing
options.c: They moved from an administrative, procedural view of managing staff to a strategic view linking people to competitive advantage
options.d: They stopped treating people as a resource and focused only on machines and capital

questions.explanation: Early definitions described HRM through operational activities such as procurement, compensation and separation, while later ones described it as strategic, aimed at sustainable competitive advantage and organisational goals. Option A reverses the direction of the change. Options B and D are wrong because later definitions place even more weight on people, not less, and clearly go beyond hiring and firing.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which definition of HRM is most closely associated with establishing the distinction between 'hard' and 'soft' HRM?

options.a: Mathis and Jackson's definition of HRM as the design of formal systems to manage human talent
options.b: Wendell L. French's definition of HRM as the recruitment, selection, development, utilisation of, and accommodation to, human resources
options.c: R. Wayne Mondy's definition of HRM as the utilisation of individuals to achieve organisational objectives
options.d: John Storey's definition of HRM as a distinctive approach to employment management seeking competitive advantage through a highly committed workforce

questions.explanation: John Storey's work is widely credited with the hard versus soft HRM distinction: hard HRM treats people mainly as a cost to be controlled, while soft HRM treats them as valued assets to be developed and committed. Options A, B and C are real definitions of HRM, but they are not the ones known for drawing this hard/soft line.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the three core elements (basic components) of any organisation?
questions.explanation: Every organisation rests on a purpose (why it exists), a structure (how roles and tasks are arranged) and people (who carry out the work). Option A lists functions of management, not elements of an organisation. Option C lists factors of production, and option B mixes parts of purpose with an outcome.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Among the three core elements of an organisation, which one is described as the driving force without which neither the purpose nor the structure can be achieved?
questions.explanation: People are the driving force: plans, organograms and policies achieve nothing unless people carry them out. Option C, structure, only arranges roles and responsibilities, and option A, purpose, is the reason the organisation exists. Option B is not one of the three core elements at all.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which function of management involves monitoring performance and taking corrective action to make sure organisational goals are met?
questions.explanation: Controlling closes the management cycle by comparing actual performance with goals and correcting any deviations. Option A, planning, sets the goals and the course of action in the first place. Option B, organising, arranges resources and activities, and option C, leading, is about directing, motivating and influencing people.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: What was the main criticism of the Classical School of management (scientific management, administrative theory and bureaucracy) in how it treated workers?

options.a: It treated workers as passive labour inputs, much like machines or other factors of production
options.b: It ignored efficiency and productivity altogether
options.c: It gave workers too much freedom to make strategic decisions
options.d: It focused mainly on workers' social and emotional needs

questions.explanation: The Classical School viewed people as inanimate labour inputs to be managed like machinery, with little regard for their psychological or social needs. Option D describes the Human Relations view, which came later as a reaction to this flaw. Options B and C are wrong because classical thinkers kept decision-making at the top and were obsessed with efficiency.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The Hawthorne experiments, which showed that workers' social and emotional needs strongly affect their performance, are associated with which school of thought?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies, led by Elton Mayo, launched the Human Relations Movement by showing that attention, group relationships and morale affect output. Options A, B and D are all branches of the earlier Classical School, which treated workers mainly as inputs to be organised efficiently.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: In the four-category classification of HRM objectives (societal, organisational, functional and personal), legal compliance, ethical employment practices and corporate social responsibility fall under which objective?
questions.explanation: The societal objective concerns HRM's responsibility to the wider society, so obeying the law, ethical employment and CSR belong here. Option A is about the individual employee, such as career growth and work-life balance. Options C and D concern the quality of the HR function itself and HR's contribution to the business.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Under the same four-category framework, career development, work-life balance and employee wellbeing are examples of which HRM objective?
questions.explanation: Personal objectives focus on the individual employee's own needs and experience, such as growth, satisfaction, wellbeing and dignity. Option D looks outward to society through legal and ethical duties. Option B covers business needs like productivity and cost management, and option A covers how well the HR department itself runs.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Within the four-category framework of HRM objectives, which objective is concerned with HR metrics and analysis, HR systems quality and HR business partnering?
questions.explanation: The functional objective is about the quality of the HR department's own operations, so its systems, metrics and partnering with business units sit here. Option A is close, but it refers to HR's contribution to the organisation as a whole, such as workforce planning, productivity and cost management. Options C and D concern employees as individuals and society at large.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which functional area of HRM is responsible for structuring pay, rewards and incentives?
questions.explanation: Compensation management designs salary structures, bonuses and other rewards. Option C sizes and plans the workforce to support strategy, and option B monitors and evaluates how well employees perform. Option D handles grievances and the general work climate rather than pay design.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which characteristic of modern HRM refers to HR working directly with executive leadership so that human capital supports the organisation's overall strategy?
questions.explanation: Strategic integration means HR sits with top leadership and builds people plans into the organisation's big-picture strategy. Option B, goal alignment, is related but refers to lining up individual workers' behaviour and outputs with corporate goals. Option D is the result of good HRM rather than the working relationship itself, and option A is a functional area, not a distinguishing characteristic.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: An MD says: 'We don't need an HRM department; a Personnel Officer who handles hiring and payroll is enough.' Which response best reflects the modern, strategic view of HRM?

options.a: HRM should replace line managers completely, so all supervision becomes HR's job
options.b: The MD is right, because HRM is simply another name for payroll administration
options.c: Hiring and payroll are necessary but not sufficient; HRM must also plan the workforce, manage performance and align people with business strategy
options.d: The MD is right, because people are factors of production to be managed like machines

questions.explanation: Strategic definitions treat HRM as aligning people with organisational strategy to achieve competitive advantage, which goes well beyond transactional hiring and payroll. Option B reduces HRM to administration, which is exactly the older personnel view being challenged. Option D repeats the classical flaw of treating workers as inputs, and option A overstates HR's role, since line managers still manage their own teams.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: A Lagos manufacturing firm's Personnel Officer handles only hiring and payroll. Which strategic HRM activity is most clearly missing from this arrangement?

options.a: Keeping employee files up to date
options.d: Workforce planning that aligns people with the firm's business strategy

questions.explanation: Strategic HRM plans the size and skills of the workforce to support where the business is going, and links people management to corporate goals. Options A, B and C are routine administrative tasks that a Personnel Officer already handles, so they are not what is missing.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: A company's HR objectives focus only on cutting recruitment costs and processing payroll on time. Using the societal, organisational, functional and personal classification of HRM objectives, which two categories are being neglected entirely?
questions.explanation: Cutting recruitment costs serves the organisational objective of cost management, and on-time payroll reflects functional HR systems quality, so those two are covered. Nothing addresses legal and ethical duties to society or employees' career growth, satisfaction and wellbeing, which are the societal and personal objectives. Options A, C and D each name at least one category the company is already serving.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: A firm's HR department meets its cost and payroll targets but ignores career development, job satisfaction and employee wellbeing. Which outcome is the most likely risk?

options.a: Higher staff turnover and lower employee engagement
options.b: Elimination of all legal compliance risks
options.d: Lower recruitment costs and faster payroll processing

questions.explanation: Neglecting the personal objective leaves employees feeling undeveloped and unvalued, which typically shows up as disengagement and people leaving. Option D describes what the firm is already achieving, not a risk. Option C is the opposite of what neglect produces, and option B is wrong because ignoring wider obligations can increase, not remove, compliance exposure.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which writer defined HRM as the planning, organising, directing and controlling of the procurement, development, compensation, integration, maintenance and separation of human resources?

options.a: Robert L. Mathis and John H. Jackson

questions.explanation: Edwin B. Flippo's classic definition lists six operative functions - procurement, development, compensation, integration, maintenance and separation - giving an operational, administrative view of managing people. Option D defined HRM simply as using individuals to achieve organisational objectives, option C is linked with the hard versus soft HRM distinction, and option A described HRM as designing formal systems to manage human talent.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The systematic process of managing people within an organisation, which involves recruiting, hiring, deploying and managing employees, is known as
questions.explanation: Human resource management is the systematic process of managing people in an organisation, covering recruiting, hiring, deploying and managing employees. Option A (workforce planning) and option B (industrial relations) are only parts of what HRM covers, while option D is about improving the whole organisation, not managing its people as such.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of human resource management?

options.a: It supports the wellbeing of employees
options.b: It treats employees mainly as interchangeable factors of production
options.d: It aligns the goals of individuals with the goals of the organisation

questions.explanation: HRM sees people as complex beings to be developed, so treating them as interchangeable factors of production is the opposite of an HRM feature; that was the flaw of the classical school. Options C, D and A are all genuine features: HRM focuses on people, aligns individual and organisational goals, and supports employee wellbeing.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which author gave the concise definition "HRM is the utilization of individuals to achieve organizational objectives"?
questions.explanation: R. Wayne Mondy's definition is the shortest of the standard definitions: HRM is simply using individuals to achieve organisational objectives. Option A (Armstrong) stressed a strategic approach to managing the organisation's most valued assets, option D (Flippo) listed six operative functions, and option C (Storey) linked HRM to competitive advantage through a committed workforce.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: "HRM is the design of formal systems in an organization to manage human talent for accomplishing organizational goals." This definition belongs to

options.b: Robert L. Mathis and John H. Jackson

questions.explanation: Mathis and Jackson define HRM in systems terms: designing formal systems to manage human talent for organisational goals. Option D (Bratton and Gold) tied HRM to sustainable competitive advantage, option C (French) listed recruitment, selection, development, utilisation and accommodation, and option A (Dessler) is known for a practical, managerial-responsibility view rather than this wording.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Bratton and Gold define HRM as a strategic approach to managing employment relations to achieve sustainable competitive advantage. Their definition is rooted in which theory of the firm?
questions.explanation: The resource-based view says a firm gains lasting advantage from valuable resources that rivals find hard to copy, and Bratton and Gold treat people as exactly such a resource. Option A and option B are classical management theories that treated workers as inputs, and option C is about the relationship between owners and managers, not people as a basis of advantage.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: John Storey's definition of HRM is especially remembered for solidifying the distinction between
questions.explanation: Storey described HRM as seeking competitive advantage through a highly committed workforce, and his work cemented the contrast between hard HRM (people as a cost to control) and soft HRM (people as an asset to develop). Option D is a separate organisational distinction, and options A and B are pairs of routine HR activities, not the conceptual split Storey is known for.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The MD of a Lagos packaging company sees staff mainly as a cost to be controlled: headcount is kept to a minimum, jobs are tightly specified and spending on training is cut whenever possible. This approach is best described as
questions.explanation: Hard HRM treats people as a cost or resource to be controlled and used efficiently, which matches tight headcount and minimal training. Option C is the opposite, treating people as valued assets to be developed, option A stresses workers' social and emotional needs, and option B is about attracting, developing and retaining talent, which this MD is neglecting.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: An Abuja software firm invests heavily in training, involves staff in decisions and tries to win their long-term commitment because it regards them as its most valuable asset. This reflects
questions.explanation: Soft HRM treats employees as valued assets whose commitment and development create advantage, which is exactly this firm's approach. Option C treats people as a cost to be controlled, option A is mainly routine record-keeping and administration, and option D saw workers as passive labour inputs.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: "A strategic approach to the management of an organization's most valued assets, the people working there, who individually and collectively contribute to the achievement of its objectives." Which author defined HRM this way?
questions.explanation: Michael Armstrong framed HRM as a strategic approach to managing people as the organisation's most valued assets, so HRM must align with business strategy. Option B and option C gave earlier, more administrative definitions built on lists of activities, and option D gave a very short 'utilization of individuals' definition.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which author defined HRM as "the recruitment, selection, development, utilization of, and accommodation to, human resources by organizations"?
questions.explanation: Wendell L. French gave this activity-based definition, which keeps HRM in an administrative, procedural mould. Options A, C and D all gave strategic definitions that link HRM to organisational strategy or competitive advantage rather than listing activities.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which author is associated with viewing HRM through the lens of managerial responsibility, with a practical and operational focus on specific functional practices?
questions.explanation: Gary Dessler's view of HRM is practical and operational, focused on what managers must actually do in specific HR practices. Option A is known for the hard versus soft distinction, option D for linking HRM to sustainable competitive advantage, and option B for describing HRM as a strategic approach.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Taken together, definitions of HRM from the 1960s to the 2000s show a general shift

options.a: From managing teams to managing individual machines and equipment
options.b: From a strategic view of managing people to a purely administrative one
options.c: From a focus on employee wellbeing to a focus on payroll only
options.d: From an administrative, procedural view of managing people to a strategic view

questions.explanation: Early definitions such as Flippo's and French's describe administrative activities, while later ones such as Armstrong's, Storey's and Bratton and Gold's treat HRM as a strategic partner tied to competitive advantage. Option B reverses the real direction of change, and options C and A describe shifts that never happened in how HRM was defined.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Career development, job satisfaction, work-life balance, employee wellbeing, and recognition and dignity are grouped under which category of HRM objectives?
questions.explanation: The personal objective focuses on the individual employee's own experience at work, including career growth, satisfaction, balance, wellbeing and dignity. Option D is about the HR function's systems, option C is about obligations to society, and option A is about organisational results.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Workforce planning, productivity enhancement, cost management, organisational development and talent acquisition are examples of which category of HRM objectives?
questions.explanation: The organisational objective is HRM's contribution to the business itself, such as planning the workforce, raising productivity, controlling cost and acquiring talent. Option C centres on the individual employee, option D on duties to society, and option B on the quality of HR's own systems and metrics.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a personal objective of HRM?
questions.explanation: Productivity enhancement is an organisational objective because it serves the business's performance rather than the individual employee. Options A, B and C are all personal objectives, centred on the employee's own growth, balance and dignity.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The HR unit of a Lagos bank introduces flexible working hours, a staff wellness programme and a clear career path for every officer. Which category of HRM objectives is it mainly pursuing?
questions.explanation: Flexible hours, wellness and career paths all serve employees' own work-life balance, wellbeing and career development, which are personal objectives. Option B would involve legal compliance or CSR, option C would involve HR systems and metrics, and option D would involve business targets such as productivity or cost.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: An HR manager in Ibadan builds a monthly dashboard that tracks staff turnover, absence rates and time-to-hire, and uses it to improve HR's own processes. Which HRM objective does this mainly serve?
questions.explanation: Tracking HR metrics to improve HR's own processes is part of the functional objective, which covers HR systems quality and HR metrics and analysis. Option D centres on employees' own needs, option C on duties to society, and option A on business-wide goals like productivity and cost.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Every organisation is said to have three basic components. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The three basic components of any organisation are people, purpose and structure; technology is a tool an organisation uses, not one of these three. Option C is the workforce that drives the organisation, option A is its reason for existing, and option D is how it assigns roles and tasks.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The element of an organisation that dictates how roles, responsibilities and tasks are assigned, shown through the organogram, processes, policies and strategic plans, is its
questions.explanation: Structure is how an organisation arranges roles, responsibilities and tasks to accomplish its purpose, and it is seen in the organogram, processes and policies. Option A is the reason the organisation exists, option D is the workforce that carries out plans, and option B is shared values and beliefs, which is not one of the three core elements.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Why are people described as the driving force of an organisation?

options.a: People decide the organisation's mission without any reference to its structure
options.b: People are the cheapest resource an organisation can obtain
options.c: People can be replaced by machines once the structure is in place
options.d: Without people to implement plans, the structure and purpose cannot be achieved

questions.explanation: People are the driving force because they are the ones who implement plans; without them, the purpose and structure exist only on paper. Option A misstates their role, option B is not the reason they matter, and option C contradicts the point that people bring creativity and judgement machines cannot replace.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The primary reason an organisation is established, defined by its mission and vision and broken down into specific objectives, is its
questions.explanation: Purpose is why the organisation exists, expressed through its mission and vision and then broken into objectives such as providing a service or earning revenue. Option B is how roles and tasks are arranged, option A is just a chart that shows the structure, and option D is an HR tool for sizing the workforce.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Directing, motivating and influencing the people within an organisation describes which management function?
questions.explanation: Leading is the people-facing function of management: directing, motivating and influencing staff. Option B is about monitoring and correcting performance, option C about structuring resources and activities, and option D about setting goals and courses of action.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which conclusion is drawn from the human relations movement about employees?

options.a: They are social and emotional assets whose wellbeing and satisfaction directly drive performance
options.b: They are inanimate factors of production like machines and capital
options.c: They are motivated only by money, so pay is the sole lever managers need
options.d: They work best when isolated from co-workers and closely timed

questions.explanation: The human relations movement showed that people are social, emotional beings and that their wellbeing and satisfaction directly affect performance. Option D is contradicted by the finding that isolating workers hurts performance, option C ignores their social needs, and option B is the classical school's view that the movement rejected.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the classical school of management?
questions.explanation: The human relations movement came after the classical school and reacted against it by stressing workers' social and emotional needs. Options B, C and D are the three branches of the classical school, which treated people as passive labour inputs.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Sizing and planning human capital so that it supports company strategies is the HRM functional area called
questions.explanation: Workforce planning means working out how many people, with what skills, the business needs to carry out its strategy. Option D structures pay and rewards, option A monitors and evaluates how employees perform, and option B handles grievances and the work environment.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Structuring pay, rewards and incentives falls under which functional area of HRM?
questions.explanation: Compensation management is the HRM area that designs pay, rewards and incentives. Option C builds skills and certifications, option B finds and hires talent, and option A sizes the workforce to fit strategy.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: At a Port Harcourt oil services firm, the HR team handles staff grievances, addresses complaints about canteen conditions and works to keep the workplace conducive. These activities belong to which HRM functional area?
questions.explanation: Employee relations and well-being covers resolving grievances, addressing staff concerns and maintaining a conducive work environment. Option B is about monitoring and evaluating performance, option C about pay and incentives, and option A about sourcing and hiring people.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The HRM functional area concerned with monitoring and evaluating how employees carry out their work is
questions.explanation: Performance management monitors and evaluates employee execution so that results can be improved. Option B deals with grievances and the work climate, option A sizes the workforce, and option C builds skills over the long term rather than evaluating current performance.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Cultivating employees' skills, capabilities and professional certifications over the long term is the HRM function of
questions.explanation: Training and development builds employees' skills and professional qualifications over time. Option C concerns pay and incentives, option B evaluates how well people perform, and option D brings new people into the organisation.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which characteristic of HRM refers to actively aligning individual workers' behaviours and outputs with corporate goals?
questions.explanation: Goal alignment is about making sure what each worker does and produces supports the company's goals. Option A is HR working with top leadership on strategy, option D is the result of executing HRM well, and option B is the skills and knowledge employees hold.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The collective skills, knowledge and abilities of employees that contribute to an organisation's value are known as
questions.explanation: Human capital is the value held in employees' skills, knowledge and abilities. Option C is the strategy for attracting and developing such people, option B is their emotional commitment, and option A is a finance term for current assets minus current liabilities.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Talent management is best defined as

options.a: Strategies to attract, develop, retain and use people with the required skills and aptitude to meet current and future organisational needs
options.b: The process of structuring pay, bonuses and incentives for top performers only
options.c: The emotional commitment an employee has to the organisation and its goals
options.d: The collective skills and knowledge of employees that add to the organisation's value

questions.explanation: Talent management covers the whole cycle of attracting, developing, retaining and using people with the right skills for present and future needs. Option C defines employee engagement, option D defines human capital, and option B describes part of compensation management.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: The emotional commitment an employee has to the organisation and its goals is called
questions.explanation: Employee engagement is the emotional commitment staff feel towards the organisation and its goals. Option C is the skills and knowledge they hold, option B is a statement of a job's required qualifications, and option A is HR's work of linking individual output to corporate goals.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: It is said that there is no best way to manage people. The reason given is that

options.a: Every organisation uses the same management methods
options.b: Labour laws forbid a single approach to managing staff
options.c: Managers are not trained in people management
options.d: People are complex beings with complex needs

questions.explanation: Because people are complex beings with complex and varied needs, no single formula works for managing all of them, and effective HRM depends on the conditions of each organisational setting. Options C, A and B are not the reason, and option A is untrue since organisations differ widely.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes human resource management from traditional personnel management?

options.a: Personnel management is broader in scope than HRM and includes business strategy
options.b: HRM is strategic and proactive, linked to business strategy, while personnel management is mainly administrative and reactive
options.c: HRM deals only with payroll and staff records, while personnel management handles strategy
options.d: They are simply two names for exactly the same function with no difference in approach

questions.explanation: Traditional personnel management focused on routine administration such as records, payroll and rules, and responded to problems as they arose, while HRM is integrated with business strategy and treats people as assets to be developed. Option A and option C reverse the two, and option D ignores the clear shift in approach.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: An officer at an Onitsha trading company spends all her time keeping staff files, processing leave forms and running payroll, and has no input into the company's business plans. Her role is closest to
questions.explanation: Routine administration such as records, leave and payroll, with no link to business strategy, is the hallmark of traditional personnel management. Option B would require her to work with top management on strategy, option D involves attracting, developing and retaining talent, and option C is planned improvement of the whole organisation.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which of the following is more characteristic of HRM than of traditional personnel management?

options.a: Viewing employees as valuable assets whose development creates competitive advantage
options.b: Keeping the people function separate from business strategy
options.c: Focusing mainly on record-keeping and compliance with staff rules
options.d: Reacting to staff problems only after they arise

questions.explanation: HRM sees people as assets to develop and links their management to competitive advantage, as in Bratton and Gold's definition. Options C, D and B describe the older personnel management approach, which was administrative, reactive and cut off from strategy.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: In most organisations, who is directly responsible for the day-to-day supervision, appraisal and coaching of the employees in a work unit?

options.a: The HR department alone, with no role for line managers
options.c: The line manager of that unit, with the HR department giving specialist support

questions.explanation: Line managers carry day-to-day people responsibilities for their own teams, such as directing, appraising and coaching, while the HR department provides policies, advice and specialist services. Option A wrongly removes line managers from people management, option B sets overall direction rather than supervising staff, and option D represents workers rather than managing them.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: A production supervisor in an Ikeja factory wants to discipline a worker for repeated lateness. What is the usual role of the HR department in this situation?

options.a: To stay out of the matter completely because discipline is not an HR issue
options.b: To take over supervising the worker permanently
options.c: To advise on the correct disciplinary policy and procedure while the supervisor handles the case
options.d: To dismiss the worker immediately without involving the supervisor

questions.explanation: The HR department plays an advisory, specialist role: it designs policies and advises line managers on handling issues like discipline fairly and legally, while the line manager deals with the employee. Option B confuses advising with supervising, option A ignores HR's role in employee relations, and option D skips both the line manager and fair procedure.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which characteristic of HRM holds that, when properly executed, HRM ensures the organisation remains competitive within its market?
questions.explanation: The competitive advantage characteristic says good HRM helps the organisation stay ahead of rivals in its market. Option C is about aligning individual output with corporate goals, option D is about HR working with top leadership on strategy, and option A is an HR functional area dealing with grievances and wellbeing.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: Which of the following is listed among the broader objectives of HRM?

options.d: Fixing the selling prices of products

questions.explanation: Knowledge retention, keeping valuable know-how inside the organisation as staff come and go, is one of HRM's broader objectives, alongside managing change and diversity and inclusion. Option B is a finance goal, option D is a marketing decision, and option C is an accounting task.

questions.topic: Nature, Scope and Importance of Human Resource Management
questions.question: HRM encompasses functions such as workforce planning, recruitment, training, performance management, compensation and employee relations. Which of the following is NOT one of these HRM functions?
questions.explanation: Designing products is an engineering or marketing task, not a people-management function. Options C, B and D are all functions HRM encompasses, together with recruitment, training and performance management.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: What is the difference between a job description and a job specification?

options.a: A job description lists the duties and responsibilities of a job, while a job specification lists the qualifications and skills needed to do it
options.b: A job description lists the qualifications needed, while a job specification lists the duties of the job
options.c: Both terms mean the same thing
options.d: A job description sets the salary, while a job specification sets working hours

questions.explanation: Job analysis produces two documents: the job description, which sets out what the job involves, and the job specification, which sets out what kind of person is needed to do it. Option B swaps the two. Option C ignores the distinction, and option D confuses them with terms of employment.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: HR forecasting shows that a firm's demand for workers will exceed the available supply. Which response is appropriate?

options.a: Freeze hiring and not replace employees who leave
options.b: Hire more workers, use overtime or subcontract some work

questions.explanation: When demand for labour exceeds supply, the firm must add capacity through hiring, overtime, subcontracting or labour-saving initiatives. Options A, C and D reduce the workforce, which is how firms respond when supply exceeds demand.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Strategic human resource planning begins with which activity?

options.a: Analysing the organisation's mission, objectives and strategy to determine what kind of people it needs

questions.explanation: HR planning starts from the organisation's mission, objectives and strategy, because the people needed depend on where the business is going. Options C and D are HR activities that come much later in the employment cycle. Option B is a financial decision, not part of HR planning.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The process of identifying the tasks, responsibilities, skills, knowledge and abilities a job requires is called:
questions.explanation: Job analysis systematically studies a job to determine what it involves and what it takes to do it, producing the job description and job specification. Option D moves employees between jobs for development. Option A evaluates how well people perform, and option C introduces new hires to the organisation.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of internal recruiting over external recruiting?

options.a: It is the only option for filling entry-level positions
options.b: It brings in fresh ideas and perspectives from outside the company
options.c: It motivates existing staff by showing chances for promotion, and the candidate's performance is already known

questions.explanation: Promoting from within signals upward mobility, is usually cheaper, and reduces risk because the organisation already knows the candidate's track record. Option B is an advantage of external recruiting. Option D is false, since moving someone internally leaves their old job empty, and option A is also false because entry-level jobs usually need external recruiting.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which of the following is a typical disadvantage of external recruiting?

options.a: It reduces the inflow of new ideas
options.b: It limits the organisation to the skills it already has
options.c: It is usually more costly and risky because the candidate is relatively unknown to the organisation

questions.explanation: External recruitment involves advertising and screening costs, and the employer has less information about how an outsider will perform. Options A and B are drawbacks of internal recruiting, which keeps the same talent pool. Option D has no basis.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: During selection, an employer contacts a candidate's former employers to confirm claims about the candidate's education and experience. This step is called:
questions.explanation: Reference checks verify what candidates say about their background before a final hiring decision. Option C happens after someone has been hired. Option D studies the job rather than the candidate, and option A evaluates existing employees.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The process of introducing new employees to the organisation's history, policies and culture, and explaining pay, benefits and how performance will be assessed, is called:
questions.explanation: Orientation welcomes new hires and explains how the organisation works and what is expected of them. Option D develops specific skills away from the workplace for existing employees. Option C prepares people to fill important future positions, and option B studies the requirements of a job.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A new machine operator learns by working alongside an experienced colleague during normal working hours. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: On-the-job training is hands-on learning while doing the actual work, often with guidance from experienced staff. Option D takes place away from daily work, for example in classrooms or workshops. Options A and B are about hiring and evaluating employees, not training them.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Why do organisations continue training employees after orientation?

options.a: Training is required only for employees who are about to be dismissed
options.b: Orientation already provides every skill an employee will ever need
options.c: Training replaces the need for recruitment
options.d: Employees rarely arrive with every skill they will need, and job requirements change over time

questions.explanation: Ongoing training and development fill skill gaps and keep employees up to date as jobs and technology change. Options A and B are false, since training serves all employees and orientation is only an introduction. Option C is wrong because training develops staff the firm already has and does not remove the need to hire.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The process of developing a plan to satisfy an organisation's human resource needs, so that it has the right number of employees with the right skills in the right places at the right times, is called
questions.explanation: Human resource planning matches the organisation's future people needs with the people it will have, in number, skills, place and time. Option B studies a single job's tasks and requirements, option A evaluates how employees have performed, and option C focuses only on filling key positions.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A job description is a written statement of

options.a: How well the current job holder has performed
options.b: The duties and responsibilities of a job
options.c: The qualifications and skills a person needs to fill the job
options.d: The salary and benefits paid to the job holder only

questions.explanation: A job description sets out what the job involves: its duties, responsibilities and reporting lines. Option C describes the job specification, which focuses on the person rather than the job, option A is a performance appraisal, and option D is only part of the reward package.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A job specification states

options.a: The performance targets the job holder must meet this year
options.b: The duties, tasks and reporting lines that make up the job
options.c: The steps the organisation follows in its selection process
options.d: The qualifications, skills and experience required of the job holder

questions.explanation: A job specification describes the kind of person needed for the job, such as qualifications, skills and experience. Option B is the job description, option C describes the selection process, and option A describes performance objectives.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A Lagos firm's document for an accountant role reads: 'B.Sc. Accounting, ICAN membership, at least three years' audit experience, good spreadsheet skills.' This document is a
questions.explanation: Listing the qualifications, membership and experience the job holder must have is what a job specification does. Option A would list the duties of the role, option D offers the job to a chosen candidate, and option B records how someone has performed.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A document for an Abuja hotel's front office supervisor states: 'Supervises six receptionists, prepares the daily occupancy report, resolves guest complaints, reports to the front office manager.' This is a
questions.explanation: Listing duties, responsibilities and the reporting line is the content of a job description. Option C would state the qualifications and experience needed, option A assesses candidates, and option D plans who will fill key roles in future.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The two main documents produced from a job analysis are

options.a: The organisation chart and the payroll register
options.b: The appraisal form and the training plan
options.c: The job description and the job specification
options.d: The offer letter and the employment contract

questions.explanation: Job analysis produces a job description, which covers the job's duties, and a job specification, which covers the qualifications the holder needs. Option D belongs to the end of selection, option B belongs to performance management and training, and option A relates to structure and pay administration.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A manufacturing firm's HR forecast shows that demand for machine operators next year will exceed the supply of available workers. Which response fits this situation?

options.b: Offering early retirement to current operators
options.d: Offering overtime or subcontracting part of the work

questions.explanation: When demand for labour exceeds supply, the firm needs more labour, so hiring, overtime, subcontracting or labour-saving initiatives are the right responses. Options B, C and A reduce the workforce, which is what a firm does when supply exceeds demand.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A Kano bank's HR forecast shows it will have more clerical staff than it needs after automating some processes. Which response is appropriate?

options.b: Subcontracting clerical work to an outside firm
options.c: Not replacing clerks who leave and offering early retirement

questions.explanation: When supply of labour exceeds demand, the firm reduces its workforce gradually through attrition, early retirement or, if needed, eliminating positions. Options D, A and B add labour, which suits a shortage, not a surplus.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The purpose of human resource supply and demand forecasting is to

options.a: Compare available workers with forecast needs to identify future hiring or job-reduction needs
options.b: Set the selling prices of the firm's labour-intensive products
options.c: Calculate the expected market demand for the firm's products next year
options.d: Measure how satisfied customers are with the service of staff

questions.explanation: HR supply and demand forecasting compares how many workers will be available with how many will be needed, so the firm knows whether to hire or reduce staff. Option C is sales forecasting, option B is a pricing decision, and option D is a marketing measure.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes recruitment from selection?

options.a: Recruitment chooses the best candidate; selection attracts applicants
options.b: Recruitment attracts a pool of suitable applicants; selection chooses the best candidate from that pool
options.c: Recruitment and selection both mean training new employees

questions.explanation: Recruitment comes first and builds a pool of qualified applicants, while selection follows and picks the most suitable person from that pool. Option A swaps the two, option C confuses them with training, and option D gets the order wrong.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Choosing the best-qualified person from a group of applicants for a job is called
questions.explanation: Selection is the step where the organisation picks the most suitable candidate from those who applied. Option A is attracting the applicants in the first place, option D introduces the new hire to the organisation after appointment, and option B is not the name of this step.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of internal recruitment?

options.a: It motivates staff by signalling upward mobility and is usually cheaper
options.b: It is the only option for entry-level roles
options.c: It always brings fresh ideas from outside the company
options.d: It never creates another vacancy to fill

questions.explanation: Filling a post from within shows staff they can grow, costs less and involves a candidate whose performance is already known. Option C is an advantage of external recruitment, option D is false because promoting someone leaves their old post empty, and option B describes when external recruitment is needed.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of internal recruitment?

options.a: It discourages staff by blocking promotion
options.b: It is always more expensive than external recruitment
options.c: It creates a new vacancy and may limit fresh ideas
options.d: The candidate's performance is completely unknown

questions.explanation: Promoting from within leaves the promoted person's old job empty and keeps the same thinking inside the firm. Option D is a drawback of external recruitment, option B reverses the usual cost advantage of internal recruitment, and option A is wrong because internal recruitment actually encourages staff.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The main advantage of external recruitment is that it

options.a: Uses candidates whose performance is already known
options.b: Is cheaper and less risky than promoting from within
options.c: Signals upward mobility to existing staff
options.d: Brings in new skills and perspectives from outside the organisation

questions.explanation: External recruitment brings in fresh skills and ideas the firm does not yet have. Option B is the opposite of the truth, since external hiring is usually costlier and riskier, and options C and A are advantages of internal recruitment.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A Lagos bank fills the vacant post of branch manager by promoting one of its experienced relationship officers. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Filling a post with an existing employee, for example by promotion, is internal recruitment. Options A, C and D all bring in people from outside the organisation.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a source of external recruitment?
questions.explanation: An internal job posting advertises a vacancy to existing staff, so it is an internal recruitment method. Options D, B and C all reach people outside the organisation.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A recruitment method in which current employees recommend friends or contacts for vacant positions is called
questions.explanation: An employee referral uses existing staff to recommend suitable candidates they know. Option C is a training method, option B uses specialist search firms to find senior people, and option D is when a job seeker turns up without being referred.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A Nigerian conglomerate pays a specialist search firm to identify and approach a suitable finance director who is currently employed by a competitor. This method is
questions.explanation: Headhunting, or executive search, uses specialist firms to find and approach senior professionals, often people already employed elsewhere. Option D targets students and fresh graduates, option B advertises to existing staff, and option C relies on staff recommendations rather than a paid search firm.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A consulting firm sets up a stand at a UNILAG career fair to recruit final-year students into its graduate trainee programme. This recruitment method is
questions.explanation: Recruiting directly from universities and career fairs is campus recruitment, commonly used for graduate trainee roles. Option B targets experienced senior people, option C uses existing staff, and option D grooms insiders for key posts.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: In a selection process made up of application, employment tests, interview, physical exam and reference checks, and final decision, which stage is used to confirm a candidate's claims about education and work experience?
questions.explanation: Reference checks verify what the candidate has claimed about qualifications and experience, while the physical exam confirms fitness for the job. Option D is only an initial screen based on what the candidate says, option A measures skills or aptitude, and option B is the choice made after checks are complete.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: In a selection process made up of application, employment tests, interview, physical exam and reference checks, and final decision, the final decision is usually made by

options.a: The line manager who will oversee the position
options.d: The newest employee in the department

questions.explanation: The final hiring decision normally rests with the line manager who will supervise the new employee, or an equivalent decision-maker, since that person must work with the hire. Options B, D and C have no role in choosing the candidate.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: In the selection process, the application form is mainly used as

options.a: The final hiring decision made by the line manager
options.b: An initial screening tool based on the candidate's education and work background
options.c: A test of the candidate's personality and temperament
options.d: A check on the candidate's physical fitness for the job

questions.explanation: The application gathers basic details about education and experience so the firm can screen out clearly unsuitable candidates early. Option A comes at the end of selection, option C is an employment test, and option D is the physical exam.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A selection test that measures a candidate's potential or ability to learn new skills is
questions.explanation: An aptitude test measures a person's capacity to learn or develop a skill, not just what they already know. Option D measures traits such as sociability or emotional stability, option A checks physical health, and option B assesses honesty.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: As part of selection for a secretarial post, candidates are asked to type a two-page letter so that their speed and accuracy can be measured. This is
questions.explanation: A work-sample or skills test asks candidates to do a real piece of the job, here typing, to measure their current ability. Option B measures traits, option A measures potential to learn rather than present skill, and option C contacts previous employers.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: An interview in which every candidate is asked the same set of predetermined questions in the same order is
questions.explanation: A structured interview uses a fixed set of questions for all candidates, which makes answers easier to compare fairly. Option D is free-flowing with no set questions, option A deliberately puts candidates under pressure, and option C is held with employees who are leaving.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: An unstructured interview is one in which

options.a: Every candidate answers exactly the same written questions
options.b: There is no fixed list of questions and the conversation flows freely
options.c: The candidate is asked only about hypothetical future situations
options.d: Several interviewers question the candidate at the same time

questions.explanation: In an unstructured interview the interviewer follows the conversation rather than a script. Option A describes a structured interview, option D a panel interview, and option C a situational interview.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A candidate for a management trainee post at a Lagos telecoms company is interviewed at the same sitting by the HR manager, the head of operations and a senior engineer. This is
questions.explanation: A panel interview has several interviewers questioning the candidate together. Option C involves only one interviewer, option A is held with staff who are leaving, and option B is a short preliminary call.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: An interviewer asks: 'Tell me about a time when you had to handle an angry customer. What did you do?' This type of interview question is
questions.explanation: Behavioural questions ask candidates how they actually behaved in past situations, on the idea that past behaviour predicts future behaviour. Option D asks what the candidate would do in a hypothetical situation, option A deliberately pressures the candidate, and option B hints at the desired answer.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: An interviewer asks: 'Suppose a customer insists on a refund that company policy does not allow. What would you do?' This is a
questions.explanation: Situational questions present a hypothetical future scenario and ask what the candidate would do. Option C asks about what the candidate actually did in the past, option B involves contacting previous employers, and option A measures traits through a written test.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A selection test is said to be valid when it

options.a: Is short and cheap to administer
options.b: Measures what it is meant to measure and predicts job performance
options.c: Gives the same results each time it is taken
options.d: Is taken by every applicant at the same time

questions.explanation: Validity means the test actually measures what it claims to measure, such as ability to do the job. Option C describes reliability, which is consistency, while options A and D are practical features, not validity.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A selection test is said to be reliable when it

options.a: Can be completed in under ten minutes
options.b: Accurately predicts how well candidates will perform on the job
options.c: Is approved by the labour ministry
options.d: Produces consistent results when repeated under similar conditions

questions.explanation: Reliability is about consistency: the same person should score about the same when tested again. Option B describes validity, and options C and A have nothing to do with how consistent the test is.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of the selection interview?

options.a: It replaces the need for any tests, reference checks or other selection steps
options.b: It is held after the new employee has worked in the firm for one year
options.c: It is used only to tell the chosen candidate what the salary will be
options.d: It lets the employer learn more about the candidate and the candidate learn about the job and organisation

questions.explanation: The interview is a two-way exchange: the employer assesses the candidate, and the candidate learns about the role and organisation. Option A is wrong since interviews sit alongside tests and checks, option C is far too narrow, and option B describes an appraisal, not selection.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: On her first day at a Lagos firm, a new graduate finds no desk ready, nobody introduces her to colleagues, and she is handed a 200-page manual to read at once. This shows

options.a: A structured selection interview held on the first day
options.b: A poorly handled orientation that can sour a new hire's first impression
options.c: A well-designed onboarding programme for graduate hires
options.d: Effective off-the-job training for new employees

questions.explanation: No workspace, no introductions and information overload are classic signs of poor orientation, which can leave a bad first impression. Option C is the opposite, option D is training held away from daily work, and option A happens before hiring.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Informal, hands-on learning that takes place while the employee is doing the actual work is
questions.explanation: On-the-job training means learning while doing the real job, often with guidance from experienced staff. Option B takes place away from the work setting, option D is the introduction for new hires, and option C studies the job itself.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Off-the-job training is best described as

options.a: Structured programmes held away from daily work distractions, often for complex or specialised skills
options.b: Introducing a new hire to company policies on the first day
options.c: Moving an employee through different jobs within the firm
options.d: Learning by watching an experienced colleague at the workstation

questions.explanation: Off-the-job training takes employees away from their normal work so they can focus on structured learning, which suits complex skills. Option D is on-the-job coaching, option C is job rotation, and option B is orientation.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A new cashier at a bank branch in Enugu learns the job by working at the counter beside an experienced teller who guides her through each transaction. This is
questions.explanation: Learning at the actual counter, while doing real transactions under guidance, is on-the-job training. Option A would take her to a classroom or training centre, option B uses a simulated work area set apart from the real one, and option D is the general introduction to the organisation.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: A manufacturing company sends its supervisors to a three-day leadership workshop at a training centre in Ibadan. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Training held away from the workplace in a structured programme is off-the-job training. Option D happens while doing the actual job, option C moves staff through different jobs, and option B is a recruitment method.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Moving an employee through a series of different jobs over a period so that they gain broad experience of the organisation is called
questions.explanation: Job rotation shifts employees from one job to another to broaden their skills and understanding. Option B adds more responsibility and challenge to the same job, option C is a statement of qualifications, and option D grooms people for specific key posts.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: In Aba, a young person spends three years learning tailoring under a master tailor, combining practical work with instruction until he can practise independently. This training method is
questions.explanation: Apprenticeship is a long period of learning a trade under an experienced master, combining instruction and practical work. Option A uses a simulated work area, option D moves staff across different jobs, and option C is a short introduction for new hires.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Vestibule training is training that

options.a: Takes place only through online courses
options.b: Consists of reading the company's history and policies
options.c: Happens at the employee's actual workstation during normal work
options.d: Takes place in a separate area set up to simulate the real work environment and equipment

questions.explanation: Vestibule training uses a training area equipped like the real workplace, so trainees can practise without disrupting actual work. Option A is e-learning, option C is on-the-job training, and option B is part of orientation.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes training from development?

options.a: Training is long-term, while development is short-term
options.b: Training is for managers only, while development is for junior staff only
options.c: Training improves skills for the current job, while development prepares employees for future roles and growth
options.d: Training and development mean exactly the same thing

questions.explanation: Training is usually short-term and focused on the present job, while development is longer-term and builds people for future responsibilities. Option B is not a real distinction, option A reverses the time focus, and option D ignores the difference.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The ongoing process by which an employee, with the organisation's support, plans and progresses through a sequence of jobs and growing responsibilities is
questions.explanation: Career development is the planned growth of an employee's career over time, supported by the organisation through training, mentoring and promotion opportunities. Option B is a one-off introduction for new staff, option D studies jobs, and option A chooses new hires.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Identifying and developing internal employees who can take over key positions when those positions become vacant is called
questions.explanation: Succession planning makes sure the organisation has prepared people ready to step into key roles when current holders leave or retire. Option D attracts applicants, often from outside, option A reduces staff numbers, and option C adds tasks to a job.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: The managing director of an Abuja firm will retire in two years. The board picks the deputy MD, gives her more responsibilities and sends her on executive programmes so that she can take over smoothly. This is
questions.explanation: Grooming a chosen insider to take over a key post when it becomes vacant is succession planning. Option C would look outside the firm, option A moves staff across many jobs for broad experience, and option D introduces new hires to the organisation.

questions.topic: HR Planning, Recruitment, Selection and Development
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of human resource planning?

options.a: Identifying shortages or surpluses of workers
options.c: Ensuring the right skills are available when needed
options.d: Setting the selling price of the firm's products

questions.explanation: Pricing products is a marketing and finance decision, not an HR planning purpose. Options B, A and C are exactly what HR planning does: forecasting needs, spotting gaps or surpluses, and making sure the right skills are available at the right time.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: Which option arranges Maslow's hierarchy of needs correctly from the lowest level to the highest?
questions.explanation: Maslow's pyramid starts with basic physiological needs such as food and shelter, then safety, social belonging, esteem, and finally self-actualisation at the top. Option A swaps the first two levels, and option B misplaces safety and esteem. Option C gives the right levels but from highest to lowest, not lowest to highest.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: According to Maslow, a factory manager who ensures that machines are guarded and the work environment is free from danger is mainly satisfying which need?
questions.explanation: Safety needs are about freedom from danger and protection, which is what a safe work environment provides. Option C refers to basic survival needs like food, water and shelter. Options B and D are higher-order needs for recognition and for reaching one's full potential.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: In Maslow's hierarchy, the need to become whatever one is capable of becoming and make full use of one's potential is called:
questions.explanation: Self-actualisation sits at the top of the hierarchy and is about achieving one's full potential. Option C is about self-confidence and being appreciated by others, which is close but still about recognition rather than growth to full potential. Options A and B are lower needs for belonging and protection.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: Which statement best captures a central principle of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?

options.a: Higher-level needs must be satisfied before physiological needs can motivate
options.b: A need that has been fully satisfied remains the strongest motivator
options.c: Lower-level needs must be largely satisfied before higher-level needs begin to motivate behaviour
options.d: All five levels of need motivate a person equally at the same time

questions.explanation: Maslow argued that people move up the pyramid: basic needs come first, and only once they are met do higher needs become the main drivers of behaviour. Option D ignores the idea of a hierarchy, and option A reverses it. Option B contradicts the principle that a satisfied need is no longer a motivator.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: In Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following is a job context (hygiene) factor rather than a job content (motivator) factor?
questions.explanation: Job context or hygiene factors surround the job, such as pay, working conditions, supervision and relationships with colleagues. Options A, B and C come from the work itself, so they are job content factors, which Herzberg called motivators.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: According to Herzberg, what happens when job context (hygiene) factors such as good working conditions and fair pay are adequately provided?

options.b: Dissatisfaction is prevented, but employees are not necessarily motivated
options.d: Employees become highly motivated to perform

questions.explanation: Hygiene factors only remove the causes of complaint: when they are missing, workers are dissatisfied, and when they are present, workers are simply not dissatisfied. Real motivation comes from job content factors such as achievement and responsibility, so option D is wrong. Option A borrows a term from Maslow, and option C is wrong because managers still need content factors to motivate.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: A manager wants to genuinely motivate staff, not just stop complaints. Following Herzberg, which action is most appropriate?

options.a: Organise more social events with colleagues
options.b: Repaint the office and improve the canteen
options.d: Give employees more challenging work, responsibility and opportunities for achievement

questions.explanation: Herzberg's motivators lie in the content of the job itself, such as challenge, responsibility, achievement and growth. Options A and B improve working conditions and interpersonal relationships, which are hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate on their own. Option C concerns supervision, which is also a hygiene factor and may even reduce satisfaction.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: A manager believes that the average employee dislikes work, avoids responsibility and must be closely supervised. This manager holds which set of assumptions?
questions.explanation: Theory X assumes people dislike work and must be controlled, which leads to an authoritarian, tightly supervising style. Option A, Theory Y, makes the opposite, positive assumptions about employees. Options C and D are separate motivation theories, not sets of managerial assumptions about human nature.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: Which leadership style is most consistent with McGregor's Theory Y assumptions?

options.a: Participative, allowing employees discretion and involvement in decisions
options.b: Bureaucratic, with no room for employee initiative
options.c: Coercive, relying on threats of punishment
options.d: Authoritarian, with close supervision and strict control

questions.explanation: Theory Y assumes people are creative, can direct themselves and accept responsibility, so a Theory Y leader extends trust and invites participation. Options B, C and D all rely on control and limit employee initiative, which fits Theory X assumptions instead.

questions.topic: Motivation, Leadership and Performance Management
questions.question: In Vroom's Expectancy Theory, the term for how attractive or desirable a particular outcome (such as a bonus or promotion) is to an individual is:
questions.explanation: Valence is the value a person places on an outcome; if the reward does not matter to the person, motivation falls. Option B, expectancy, is the belief that effort will lead to good performance, and option A, instrumentality, is the belief that good performance will lead to the outcome.
