questions.question: Any significant alteration in the structure, operations, culture, technology, strategies or processes of an organisation, moving it from its current state to a desired future state, is called
questions.explanation: Organisational change is any significant alteration in how the organisation is set up or operates, taking it from where it is to where it wants to be. Option D is shared values and beliefs, option B is the arrangement of roles and reporting lines, and option A is the process of setting long-term goals, which may lead to change but is not the change itself.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: The systematic process of planning, implementing, monitoring and sustaining organisational change so that it is introduced smoothly with minimal disruption is
questions.explanation: Change management is the deliberate process of planning, carrying out, monitoring and sustaining a change. Option C is the change itself rather than how it is managed, option D is people's unwillingness to accept change, and option B is one particular kind of personnel change.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of organisational change?

options.a: It may be planned or unplanned
options.b: It is influenced by internal and external factors
options.c: It occurs only once in the life of an organisation

questions.explanation: Organisational change is continuous, not a one-off event, because the environment keeps changing. Options D, A and B are genuine characteristics, along with being necessary for survival and affecting employees positively or negatively.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A Nigerian beverage company decides to enter the Ghanaian market and introduce a new line of products. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Strategic change involves changes made to achieve long-term goals, such as entering new markets or launching new products. Option A is about departments and reporting lines, option C about recruitment, promotion or downsizing, and option D about values and attitudes.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A firm merges its sales and marketing departments and changes who reports to whom. This is
questions.explanation: Structural change alters the organisation's structure, for example by creating or merging departments and changing reporting relationships. Option A involves new equipment or systems, option D involves values and beliefs, and option C involves long-term goals such as new markets.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A bank in Lagos replaces manual ledgers with computerised accounting and introduces online banking. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Introducing new technology or equipment, such as computerised accounting, online banking, automation or AI, is technological change. Option C concerns staff movements, option D concerns departments and reporting lines, and option B concerns values and attitudes.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Management at an Abuja firm tries to get staff to value teamwork instead of competing against one another individually. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Cultural change alters the organisation's values, beliefs and attitudes, such as promoting teamwork over individual competition. Option A would change departments or reporting lines, option D would introduce new equipment, and option B would involve hiring, promoting or laying off people.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Recruitment, promotion, training, downsizing and retirement are examples of which type of organisational change?
questions.explanation: Personnel change involves changes to the people in the organisation, such as who is hired, promoted, trained or released. Option A concerns long-term goals and markets, option B values and beliefs, and option C new equipment and systems.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A newly appointed MD at a Port Harcourt firm introduces a new set of policies within her first month. As a driver of change, this is best classified as
questions.explanation: New leadership originates within the organisation, so it is an internal driver; a new manager often brings different policies. Options A, D and C are all forces from outside the organisation.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Rising inflation and a sharp fall in the naira exchange rate force a Lagos importer to cut costs and restructure. This driver of change is

options.d: Financial problems caused by new leadership, an internal driver

questions.explanation: Inflation, recession and exchange rate movements are economic conditions that come from outside the firm and may require cost-cutting. Options D, C and A are internal drivers that originate within the organisation, and none of them describes what triggered this change.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: The business environment in which organisations operate is characterised as
questions.explanation: The business environment keeps changing, has many sides and is complex, which is why organisations must keep adapting. Options C, A and D describe a stable environment in which change management would hardly be needed.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a factor that brings about organisational change?

options.c: The emergence of a knowledge workforce

questions.explanation: The rise of a knowledge workforce is one of the listed factors that push organisations to change, along with competition, technology, regulation and globalisation. Options B, A and D describe conditions that would reduce the need for change, not cause it.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: When an organisation grows and its employees need new knowledge and abilities, the change is in the area of employee skills. This is mainly addressed through
questions.explanation: Change in employee skills means staff must learn new knowledge and abilities, so change management uses training and development programmes. Option A is a branding decision, option B a pricing decision, and option C a structural change.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: In which area of organisational change does management mainly use communication, motivation and involvement to encourage positive attitudes and teamwork towards the change?
questions.explanation: Change in employee attitude targets staff willingness to accept and support change, and organisations shape it through communication, motivation and involvement. Option C concerns adopting new tools and software, option A concerns departments and reporting lines, and option D concerns the long-term plan.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Field's (2006) third level of organisational change is best described as

options.a: A minor change to the daily procedures of one department only
options.b: A strategic questioning of purpose and agenda limited to top management
options.c: An organisation-wide effort involving order, beliefs, values and the relationships among subsystem groups
options.d: An implemental adjustment that keeps the existing alignment of the system

questions.explanation: The third level is the broadest: an organisation-wide effort touching order, beliefs, values and how the subsystems relate. Option D is the first level, option B resembles the second level, and option A is too narrow for any but the first level.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: The unwillingness of employees or organisations to accept new ideas, methods, policies or procedures is called
questions.explanation: Resistance to change is the reluctance to accept new ideas, methods, policies or procedures, often because people fear uncertainty. Option B is the process of managing change, option A is Lewin's final stage that makes change permanent, and option D is not a recognised term.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: When a Lagos bottling plant announces it will install automated packing lines, the packers protest because they worry the machines will replace them. The main cause of their resistance is
questions.explanation: Workers who worry automation will take their jobs are resisting out of fear of job loss. Option B would apply if the change made them work harder, option C if they simply preferred old routines, and option D if weak leaders were the problem.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Staff at a firm keep using the old filing system even though a better one has been introduced, saying they are simply used to the old way. Their resistance arises from
questions.explanation: Habit makes people comfortable with existing routines, so they resist even a better new method. Option D would involve worry about being replaced, option C doubts about management's motives, and option B complaints that the change means more work.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Older clerks at an Ibadan insurance company avoid the new computer system because they fear they do not have the computer skills to operate it. This cause of resistance is
questions.explanation: Fearing that one cannot use the new technology is resistance due to lack of skills, which training can address. Option C concerns extra work, option D weak leaders, and option A doubts about management's honesty or motives.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an effect of resistance to change?
questions.explanation: Resistance slows change down; delays in implementation are one of its effects, so faster implementation is not. Options A, D and C are listed effects, along with employee dissatisfaction and reduced organisational performance.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: As a way of managing resistance to change, counselling is used mainly to

options.a: Give employees the technical skills to use new systems
options.b: Reward employees who support the change
options.c: Explain to employees why the change is necessary
options.d: Help employees adjust emotionally to the change

questions.explanation: Counselling helps employees cope emotionally with the change. Option A describes training, option B describes rewards, and option C describes effective communication.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Before introducing a new shift system, the manager of a Kano factory holds meetings where workers suggest how the shifts should be organised, and many suggestions are adopted. Which method of reducing resistance is being used?
questions.explanation: Allowing employees to contribute ideas is employee participation, which builds ownership of the change. Option A forces change through threats, option B helps people adjust emotionally, and option C recognises those who support the change after the fact.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: In Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to overcoming resistance, a company that offers a union an improved severance package in return for the union's agreement to a restructuring is using
questions.explanation: Negotiation and agreement means offering something of value in exchange for acceptance of the change, as with the severance package here. Option C relies on explaining the change, option A on emotional and practical support, and option D on threats or force.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: In Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to overcoming resistance, a manager who tells staff that anyone who refuses to adopt the new system will be transferred or lose their job is using
questions.explanation: Coercion forces acceptance by threatening job loss, transfer or other penalties; it is fast but risky because it breeds resentment. Option D involves staff in designing the change, option B gives resisters a token role or selective information, and option C offers incentives in exchange for agreement.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: In Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to overcoming resistance, giving the leader of a group of resisters a visible but largely symbolic role on the change committee in order to win his endorsement is
questions.explanation: Co-optation gives a resistance leader a desirable role mainly to gain his endorsement, not to use his ideas, which is why it falls under manipulation and co-optation. Option D relies on explaining the case for change, option B on training and emotional support, and option C on genuinely using staff input in designing the change.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of effective change management?

options.a: It improves employee confidence during the change
options.b: It minimises disruptions to normal operations
options.c: It reduces employee resistance to the change
options.d: It guarantees that no employee will ever object to any change

questions.explanation: Change management reduces resistance but cannot guarantee that nobody will ever object. Options C, B and A are real benefits, along with improving communication, ensuring successful implementation and increasing competitiveness.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: In the six-step change management process (identify the need, plan, communicate, implement, monitor progress, reinforce), the step that ensures the new practices become permanent is
questions.explanation: Reinforcing the change, the final step, makes sure the new practices stick and become permanent. Option D checks whether objectives are being achieved, option B informs employees of the reasons and benefits, and option A develops objectives and implementation strategies.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Which option gives the steps of the six-step change management process in the correct order?

options.a: Identify the need, plan, communicate, implement, monitor progress, reinforce
options.b: Identify the need, implement, plan, communicate, monitor progress, reinforce
options.c: Communicate, identify the need, plan, monitor progress, implement, reinforce
options.d: Plan, identify the need, implement, communicate, reinforce, monitor progress

questions.explanation: The process starts by identifying why change is needed, then planning it, communicating it, implementing it, monitoring progress and finally reinforcing it. Option D plans before knowing the need, option B implements before planning, and option C communicates before the need is even identified.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A Lagos hospital has just launched a new electronic records system and is now checking, week by week, whether waiting times have fallen as planned. In the six-step change management process, which step is this?
questions.explanation: Checking whether objectives are being achieved after implementation is the monitor progress step. Option C comes at the very start, option A comes last and makes the change permanent, and option D comes before implementation.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: In Lewin's change model, the unfreezing stage involves

options.a: Establishing new policies and rewarding compliance
options.b: Preparing employees by explaining the need for change, creating awareness and reducing resistance
options.c: Introducing the new technology and training staff to use it

questions.explanation: Unfreezing prepares people for change by explaining why it is needed, building awareness and lowering resistance. Option C belongs to the changing stage, option A to refreezing, and option D is a step in Kotter's model.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A company installs a fingerprint attendance machine and trains all staff on how to clock in with it. In Lewin's model, this is the
questions.explanation: The changing stage is where implementation actually happens, such as introducing new technology and providing training. Option B comes before, explaining why the change is needed, option C comes after, making the change permanent, and option D is Kotter's final step, not a Lewin stage.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Six months after a new procurement system was introduced at an Abuja agency, management writes it into the official policy manual and gives awards to units that follow it fully. In Lewin's model, this is the
questions.explanation: Refreezing makes the change permanent by establishing new policies, rewarding compliance and reinforcing new behaviour. Option C prepares people before the change, option B is the implementation itself, and option A relates to Kotter's first step.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Before introducing new accounting software, management at an Enugu firm holds a meeting to explain why the old system can no longer cope and why the change is necessary. In Lewin's model, this is the
questions.explanation: Explaining why the change is needed, to prepare people and reduce resistance, is unfreezing. Option D is when the software is actually introduced, option A is when the new way is made permanent, and option B is a Kotter step.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Lewin's force field analysis explains change in terms of

options.a: Driving forces that push for change and restraining forces that resist it

questions.explanation: Force field analysis sees the current situation as a balance between driving forces for change and restraining forces against it; change happens when driving forces are strengthened or restraining forces weakened. Option D is Herzberg's theory, option C is Vroom's theory, and option B is a classification of managerial decisions.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: In Kotter's eight-step model, which step comes immediately after 'communicate the vision'?
questions.explanation: After the vision is communicated (step 4), the next step is to remove obstacles (step 5) that hinder the change. Option B is step 6, option A is step 3, and option C is step 2.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: The final step in Kotter's eight-step model is to

options.a: Anchor the change in the organisation's culture

questions.explanation: Kotter's last step anchors the change by making the new practices part of the organisational culture. Option D is step 7, option C is step 1, and option B is the final stage of Lewin's model, not Kotter's.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Three months into a branch modernisation programme, the CEO of a Nigerian bank publicly celebrates the first two branches that cut customer waiting time in half. In Kotter's model, this is
questions.explanation: Celebrating early, visible successes to build momentum is the short-term wins step. Option C comes first and shows why change is needed, option B comes last and embeds the change in the culture, and option D sets out the picture of the future.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of Kotter's eight-step model?

options.a: It is too simple for large organisations
options.b: It assumes change has a clear end with no further steps
options.c: It ignores the need to communicate a vision
options.d: It is time-consuming and requires strong leadership

questions.explanation: Kotter's model is detailed, so it takes time, needs strong leadership and is hard to apply in very unstable environments. Options A and B are criticisms of Lewin's model, and option C is false because communicating the vision is one of Kotter's steps.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A person or group who initiates, guides and takes responsibility for managing change in an organisation is called

options.b: A guiding coalition of shareholders only

questions.explanation: A change agent is anyone, inside or outside the organisation, who acts as a catalyst for change and manages the change process. Option B is wrong because Kotter's guiding coalition is a team of influential people, not shareholders only, option A controls the flow of information, and option C is not a recognised term.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A Lagos manufacturer hires an outside consulting firm as its change agent instead of using one of its own managers. Which is the main advantage and the main drawback of this choice?

options.a: Advantage: no cost at all; drawback: too much loyalty to current managers
options.b: Advantage: deep knowledge of the firm's history; drawback: lack of objectivity
options.c: Advantage: guaranteed staff acceptance; drawback: no new ideas
options.d: Advantage: a more objective, fresh view; drawback: less knowledge of the firm's culture, history and people

questions.explanation: External change agents bring objectivity and new ideas because they are not tied to internal politics, but they lack an insider's knowledge of the organisation's culture and people. Option B describes an internal change agent, option A is wrong because consultants are paid and are not bound to current managers, and option C wrongly promises acceptance and denies the fresh perspective outsiders bring.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: A Nigerian firm's change programme keeps stalling because frequent shifts in government policy and high inflation repeatedly upset its cost plans. These challenges are best described as

options.c: Unstable government policies and economic instability
options.d: Resistance from employees and inadequate training

questions.explanation: Frequent policy shifts and high inflation are the challenges of unstable government policies and economic instability that Nigerian organisations face during change. Options D, B and A are also real challenges in Nigeria, but none of them describes what is happening in this scenario.

questions.topic: Organisational Change and Change Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended strategy for managing change in Nigerian organisations?

options.a: Building trust between management and employees
options.c: Keeping change plans secret from staff until implementation is complete
options.d: Training employees regularly on new systems

questions.explanation: Hiding plans from staff undermines communication and trust, which are central to managing change well. Options D, B and A are recommended strategies, alongside improving communication, investing in technology, strengthening leadership, developing flexible policies and rewarding innovation.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Decisions that translate top management's direction into departmental plans that units can implement are called:

options.a: Strategic decisions, made by top management
options.b: Tactical decisions, made by middle-level managers
options.c: Programmed decisions, made by any employee
options.d: Operational decisions, made by first-line managers

questions.explanation: Tactical decisions sit in the middle: departmental heads and middle managers break the organisation's overall direction into workable plans. Option A sets that overall direction in the first place. Option D covers day-to-day running, and option C describes routine decisions handled by rules, which is a different way of classifying decisions.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A company's board and CEO decide whether to diversify into a new industry. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Strategic decisions concern the long-term direction of the whole organisation, such as which industry to operate in or whether to expand or diversify, and they are made at the top. Options B and C are made lower down to implement plans or run daily operations. Option A is wrong because diversification is unique and complex, not routine.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A supervisor decides how to allocate today's shifts among workers on the shop floor. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Operational decisions deal with the day-to-day running of the organisation and are made by first-line managers and supervisors. Option A concerns long-term direction, and option B concerns turning strategy into departmental plans. Option D is wrong because shift allocation is routine and familiar, not unique and complex.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A bag contains 100 balls: 40 red and 60 black. A decision-maker must bet on drawing a red ball. Because the outcomes and their probabilities are known, this situation is one of:
questions.explanation: Risk exists when the possible outcomes can be identified and their probabilities can be estimated, here a 40 percent chance of red. Option D would apply if the mix of balls were not disclosed, so no meaningful probability could be assigned. Option A is wrong because the outcome is still unknown, and option C describes limits on decision-makers, not a decision condition.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A sudden national lockdown, which no one had expected and to which no reliable probability could have been assigned in advance, is an example of decision-making under:
questions.explanation: Uncertainty exists when possible outcomes are hard to identify and reliable probabilities cannot be calculated, as with an unexpected lockdown. Option B requires probabilities that can reasonably be estimated, for example from past experience. Options A and D wrongly suggest the outcome was known or routine.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Why is insurance possible for many business hazards?

options.a: Because the hazards are programmed decisions
options.b: Because insurers know exactly which firms will suffer losses
options.c: Because they involve uncertainty, where no probability can be estimated
options.d: Because they involve risk, whose probability can be estimated from past experience

questions.explanation: Insurers price policies by estimating the likelihood of losses from past data, which is only possible when a situation involves risk. Option C is the opposite: true uncertainty cannot be priced. Option B confuses estimating probabilities with knowing outcomes, and option A misuses a term for routine decisions.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Which of the following is an assumption of the rational decision-making model?

options.a: The decision-maker settles for the first option that is good enough
options.b: The decision-maker relies mainly on feelings and personal relationships
options.c: The decision-maker has complete information and can identify and evaluate all alternatives
options.d: The decision-maker's information and time are always limited

questions.explanation: The rational model assumes a clear grasp of the problem, complete information, all alternatives identified, consequences evaluated accurately and the best option chosen. Option A describes satisficing under bounded rationality. Option B is the opposite of the model's objective, fact-based approach, and option D is a limitation of the model rather than one of its assumptions.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Why is the rational decision-making model often described as an ideal rather than a full description of how managers actually decide?

options.b: Because it has no structured steps
options.c: Because managers rarely have complete information, unlimited time or unlimited resources
options.d: Because it ignores the need to evaluate alternatives

questions.explanation: In real life managers face incomplete information, time pressure and scarce resources, so they cannot always follow every step perfectly. Options A, B and D are wrong because the model's strengths are exactly that it reduces impulsive decisions, gives a structured process and requires systematic evaluation of alternatives.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The idea that decision-makers face limits such as incomplete information, limited cognitive capacity and time pressure is known as:
questions.explanation: Bounded rationality recognises that human reasoning operates within real limits, so managers cannot always find the perfect answer. Options A and B are specific biases that distort judgement. Option D refers to routine decisions handled by rules and procedures.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A manager stops searching once she finds a supplier that meets her minimum requirements, instead of evaluating every possible supplier. This behaviour is called:
questions.explanation: Satisficing means choosing an option that is good enough or satisfactory rather than the absolute best, a natural response to bounded rationality. Option D is what the rational model assumes, choosing the best possible option. Options A and C are biases: over-reliance on first information, and sticking with a failing course because of past investment.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A manager keeps pouring money into a failing project because 'we have already spent too much to stop now.' Which bias is this?
questions.explanation: Escalation of commitment is continuing a failing course of action because of resources already invested, the sunk-cost trap. Option D is over-reliance on the first piece of information received. Option A is judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind, and option B is overestimating one's own knowledge or ability.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: During salary negotiations, a manager keeps relying on the first figure mentioned, even after better market data becomes available. Which bias is this?
questions.explanation: Anchoring bias is relying too heavily on the first information received, even when better information appears later. Option D is seeking information that supports an existing belief. Option A concerns continuing a failing investment, and option B concerns judging probability by how memorable examples are.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: People often fear shark attacks more than being hit by falling coconuts, simply because shark scenes are more vivid and memorable. Which bias does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Availability bias is judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, often because they are recent or vivid, rather than by actual probability. Option A is about over-relying on first information. Option C is about seeking supporting evidence for an existing belief, and option D is about overestimating ability.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A manager who believes a new product will succeed reads only reports that support this view and ignores evidence that contradicts it. Which bias is this?
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek information that supports an existing belief while disregarding contradicting evidence. Option D is about how easily examples come to mind. Option B involves continuing to invest because of past spending, and option C is over-reliance on the first information received.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: In the eight-step managerial decision-making process, which step comes immediately after diagnosing the problem?
questions.explanation: After identifying and diagnosing the problem, the manager sets the criteria, such as cost, quality, speed or risk, that will be used to judge alternatives. Option B comes next, once criteria exist. Options A and D come later still, after alternatives have been evaluated.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: What is the final step of the eight-step managerial decision-making process?

options.a: Evaluating the outcome of the decision

questions.explanation: The process ends by evaluating the outcome: did the decision solve the problem, were there unintended consequences, and what should change? Option B is the seventh step, just before evaluation. Option D is the sixth step, and option C is the very first step.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A firm's sales have dropped. Before choosing a solution, the manager investigates what changed, when it changed and which department is involved, treating the drop as a symptom. Which step is the manager carrying out?
questions.explanation: Diagnosing the problem means investigating its root causes rather than reacting to surface symptoms, just as a headache is a symptom and not the underlying illness. Option B happens only after a decision has been implemented. Options A and D come later, after the true problem and decision criteria are clear.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The process of identifying a choice among alternative courses of action is known as
questions.explanation: Decision-making is the process of identifying a choice among alternative courses of action, so it always involves picking between options. Option D is about setting objectives, which uses decisions but is a wider management function. Option B is only one step inside the decision process, where causes are investigated.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A decision situation exists when certain conditions are present. Which of the following is NOT one of those conditions?

options.a: More than one course of action is possible
options.b: All the relevant information about every option is available
options.c: A choice among the courses of action must be made
options.d: A problem or opportunity has been identified

questions.explanation: A decision exists when a problem or opportunity is identified, more than one course of action is possible and a choice must be made. Complete information is not required; in fact managers rarely have it, which is why bounded rationality exists. Options D, A and C are exactly the three conditions.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The owner of a Yaba bakery has only one supplier of flour in the area and no other way to get flour. Strictly speaking, why is there no real decision to make about the flour supplier?

options.b: No problem or opportunity has been identified
options.c: The situation involves risk rather than certainty
options.d: Only one course of action is possible

questions.explanation: A decision requires more than one possible course of action; with only one supplier and no alternative, there is nothing to choose between. Option B is wrong because the need for flour is clearly identified. Option A is wrong because incomplete information does not stop a decision from existing; it only makes it harder.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: When decision-making is linked to the four functions of management, the question 'What corrective action is required?' belongs to which function?
questions.explanation: Controlling compares results with plans and decides what corrective action is required. Option C asks what objectives should be pursued, option D asks how resources should be arranged, and option A asks how employees should be motivated.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Which pairing of a management function with its typical decision question is CORRECT?

options.a: Planning - What corrective action is required?
options.b: Organising - How should resources be arranged?
options.c: Controlling - How should employees be motivated?
options.d: Leading - Which objectives should be pursued?

questions.explanation: Organising is about arranging resources, so its decision question is how resources should be arranged. Option A wrongly gives planning the controlling question; planning asks which objectives to pursue. Options D and C also swap the questions between functions.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of strategic decisions?

options.a: They are associated with significant uncertainty
options.b: They are routine and easy to reverse

questions.explanation: Strategic decisions are long-term, complex, often difficult to reverse and associated with significant uncertainty. Being routine and easy to reverse is the opposite, and describes programmed day-to-day decisions. Options D, C and A are all genuine characteristics of strategic decisions.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The board of a Lagos-based fintech decides to expand operations into Ghana and Kenya over the next five years. This is best classified as
questions.explanation: Deciding whether to expand or diversify concerns the overall long-term direction of the company and is taken by the board, so it is strategic. Option A would be how each department plans to support the expansion. Option B is wrong because a first-time expansion is unique and unfamiliar, not routine.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: After the board of a Nigerian supermarket chain decides to grow market share, the head of marketing draws up a six-month departmental promotion plan to support that goal. The head of marketing's decision is
questions.explanation: Tactical decisions translate strategic objectives into departmental plans and are made by middle managers or heads of departments. Option B is the board's original choice to grow market share. Option D would be day-to-day matters such as which cashier works which shift.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A shift supervisor at a Dangote cement depot decides which loaders will work the morning shift today. This is
questions.explanation: Operational decisions concern the day-to-day functioning of the organisation and are made by supervisors and frontline managers. Option B is about long-term direction set at the top. Option C is a middle-level departmental plan, not a daily staffing choice.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Non-programmed decisions are best described as decisions that are

options.a: made only by first-line managers on a daily basis
options.b: unique, complex and unfamiliar, requiring judgement, creativity and analysis
options.c: routine and repetitive, handled by standard operating procedures
options.d: made by following rules written in the staff handbook

questions.explanation: Non-programmed decisions are unique, complex and unfamiliar, so no ready rule exists and managers must use judgement, creativity and analysis. Options C and D describe programmed decisions. Option A wrongly ties them to one level; first-line managers mostly make routine decisions.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A bank's staff handbook states exactly how many days of annual leave each grade of staff receives. A request for annual leave handled under this rule is an example of
questions.explanation: Leave requests are routine and repetitive, and the handbook already sets the rule, so this is a programmed decision. Option B would apply to a new, unfamiliar problem with no rule. Option D concerns long-term direction, not routine staff administration.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: In the eight-step managerial decision-making process, which step comes immediately AFTER establishing decision criteria?
questions.explanation: The order is identify, diagnose, establish criteria, generate alternatives, evaluate alternatives, select, implement and evaluate the outcome. So once criteria are set, alternatives are generated. Option D cannot come next because there is nothing to evaluate until alternatives exist; option A comes before the criteria.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Which of the following shows the correct order of these four steps of the decision-making process?

options.a: Establish decision criteria - Diagnose the problem - Implement the decision - Evaluate alternatives
options.b: Evaluate alternatives - Diagnose the problem - Establish decision criteria - Implement the decision
options.c: Diagnose the problem - Establish decision criteria - Evaluate alternatives - Implement the decision
options.d: Diagnose the problem - Evaluate alternatives - Establish decision criteria - Implement the decision

questions.explanation: Causes are diagnosed first, then criteria are set, then alternatives are evaluated against those criteria, and only then is the chosen option implemented. Option D evaluates alternatives before criteria exist, which is impossible because alternatives are judged by the criteria. Options A and B also put diagnosis in the wrong place.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The step of the decision-making process in which the manager investigates the causes of the problem is called
questions.explanation: Diagnosis means investigating the causes, for example what changed, when and in which department. Option A only notices that something needs attention. Option B decides which factors will be used to judge options.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Sales at a Kano beverage distributor have fallen for three months. The manager first says, 'The fall in sales is only what we can see; I need to find what is really causing it.' Which idea is the manager applying?

options.c: Distinguishing symptoms from the underlying problem

questions.explanation: A drop in sales is a symptom, not the problem itself, so a good manager looks past it to the root cause, just as headache is a symptom of malaria. Option B is continuing a failing course because of past investment. Option D is accepting a good-enough choice, which is not what the manager is doing here.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: In the decision-making process, 'establishing decision criteria' means

options.a: checking whether the decision solved the problem
options.b: determining what factors will be used to evaluate alternatives
options.c: choosing the option considered most appropriate
options.d: listing every possible course of action

questions.explanation: Decision criteria are the factors, such as cost, quality, speed, risk and ethics, against which alternatives will be judged. Option D is generating alternatives. Option C is selecting an alternative and option A is evaluating the outcome.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Implementing a decision requires several things. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: Implementation requires resources, communication, responsibility and timelines so that the chosen option is actually carried out. Shareholder approval is not a general requirement for implementing managerial decisions. Options D, B and C are all listed requirements.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A state government rewards a young man with a car for rescuing a child from a canal. Within weeks, several people stage fake rescues hoping for similar rewards. The fake rescues are best described as
questions.explanation: The government did not plan for copycat stunts, so they are unintended consequences, which the final step of evaluating outcomes is meant to catch. Option A refers to factors used to judge alternatives before choosing. Option C means accepting a good-enough option, which is unrelated.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The rational decision-making model is often presented as which sequence?

options.a: Choice - Problem identification - Alternatives - Evaluation - Implementation - Evaluation
options.b: Problem identification - Alternatives - Evaluation - Choice - Implementation - Evaluation
options.c: Problem identification - Choice - Alternatives - Implementation - Evaluation - Evaluation
options.d: Alternatives - Problem identification - Choice - Evaluation - Implementation - Evaluation

questions.explanation: The model moves logically from identifying the problem to listing alternatives, evaluating them, choosing, implementing and finally evaluating results. Option C makes the choice before alternatives exist. Options D and A also start in the wrong place.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Which of the following is a strength of the rational decision-making model?

options.a: It lets managers rely on gut feeling when data is scarce
options.b: It encourages systematic analysis and reduces impulsive decisions
options.c: It assumes managers have limited time and information
options.d: It removes the need to evaluate the outcome afterwards

questions.explanation: The rational model encourages systematic analysis, reduces impulsive decisions and provides a structured process. Option C is the opposite of its assumptions. Option A is not a feature of a fact-based model, and option D is wrong because the model ends with evaluation.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The concept of bounded rationality is associated with
questions.explanation: Herbert Simon introduced bounded rationality, the idea that decision-makers work under limits such as incomplete information and limited cognitive capacity. Option A is known for the principles and functions of management. Option B is known for the hierarchy of needs and option C for the unfreeze-change-refreeze change model.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Selecting an option that is good enough or satisfactory, because the absolute best solution cannot be identified, is called
questions.explanation: Satisficing means settling for a satisfactory, good-enough option, which is what managers do under bounded rationality. Option B means finding the single best solution, which the rational model assumes. Option A is a bias about continuing a failing project.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Bounded rationality recognises that decision-makers operate under limitations. Which of the following is NOT one of those limitations?
questions.explanation: Bounded rationality lists incomplete information, limited cognitive capacity, time pressure, uncertainty and organisational constraints. Unlimited access to reliable information is the opposite of a limitation; it is an assumption of the rational model. Options C, A and D are all genuine limitations.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A procurement officer at a Port Harcourt oil-servicing firm needs a generator within two days. She checks three vendors and buys from the first one that meets the budget and power rating, without searching further. Her approach is an example of

options.b: the rational model's search for the best option

questions.explanation: Under time pressure she accepts the first option that meets her minimum standards, which is satisficing, a direct result of bounded rationality. Option B would require identifying and comparing all alternatives to find the best. Option C involves sticking with a failing course because of past investment, which is not the case here.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The tendency to seek information that supports one's existing beliefs is called
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is seeking information that supports what you already believe while disregarding contradicting evidence. Option D is relying too heavily on the first information received. Option C is relying on information that is easily recalled.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A supplier first quotes N9 million for a delivery van. Even after the admin manager learns that similar vans sell for about N6 million, he negotiates only down to N8.5 million, still treating N9 million as his reference point. This illustrates
questions.explanation: The first quote of N9 million anchored his judgement, so he relied too heavily on it even after better price information became available. Option D would involve a vivid, easily recalled example. Option A would involve continuing to pour money into a failing project.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A Nigerian logistics company has already spent N40 million on a tracking app that keeps failing. The MD approves another N15 million, arguing, 'We have spent too much to stop now.' Which bias is this?
questions.explanation: Escalation of commitment is continuing to invest in a failing project because resources have already been invested; the N40 million is a sunk cost. Option D is about over-relying on the first information received. Option B is about seeking only supporting information, which is not the MD's stated reason.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: After a widely shared video of a robbery at an ATM, a branch manager concludes that ATM robberies are now the bank's biggest risk, although records show card fraud causes far greater losses. This illustrates
questions.explanation: Availability bias is judging likelihood by how easily a vivid or recent example comes to mind rather than by actual probability, like fearing shark attacks more than falling coconuts. Option B would require sticking to the first piece of information received. Option C is overestimating one's own knowledge or ability.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A new sales manager in Abuja refuses to look at market research because he is sure his ten years of experience tell him exactly what customers want. He is showing
questions.explanation: Overconfidence bias is the tendency to overestimate one's own knowledge or ability, which leads him to dismiss data. Option B would involve relying on an easily recalled event. Option A would involve relying on the first information he received.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: In decision-making, a situation of RISK exists when

options.a: the manager has no information at all about the future
options.b: the outcome of every alternative is known in advance
options.c: possible outcomes are difficult to identify and probabilities cannot be calculated
options.d: possible outcomes can be identified and their probabilities can reasonably be estimated

questions.explanation: Risk exists when the possible outcomes are known and probabilities can reasonably be estimated, for example from past experience, which is why insurance can exist. Option C defines uncertainty. Option B describes certainty, where there is no doubt about outcomes.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A decision is said to be made under conditions of CERTAINTY when

options.a: neither the outcomes nor their probabilities can be identified
options.b: the decision is routine and covered by a staff handbook
options.c: probabilities of outcomes can be estimated but the result is unknown
options.d: the decision-maker knows the exact outcome of each alternative in advance

questions.explanation: Certainty means the outcome of each alternative is known, for example a fixed-rate deposit with a guaranteed return. Option C describes risk and option A describes uncertainty. Option B describes a programmed decision, which is a different classification.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Bag A contains 100 balls: 40 red and 60 black. Bag B also contains 100 red and black balls, but the mix is not disclosed. A player who must guess the colour drawn from Bag B faces

options.a: certainty, because there are only two colours
options.b: risk, because the probabilities are known exactly
options.c: risk, because there are 100 balls in the bag
options.d: uncertainty, because no meaningful probability can be assigned

questions.explanation: With Bag B the ratio is hidden, so no meaningful probability can be assigned, which is uncertainty. Bag A is the risk case, because the 40:60 ratio lets you estimate a probability. Option A is wrong because knowing there are two colours does not tell you the outcome.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Which of the following events is best classified as UNCERTAINTY rather than risk for a Nigerian business?

options.a: A sudden pandemic lockdown that no one expected
options.b: A 30% chance of rain on an outdoor event based on weather data
options.c: A 5% chance of fire damage estimated from insurance records
options.d: A 2% default rate on loans calculated from past borrowers

questions.explanation: A sudden lockdown like the COVID-19 one was unexpected, with outcomes hard to identify and no reliable probability, so it is uncertainty. Options C, B and D all have probabilities estimated from records or data, which makes them risk.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A Lagos events company estimates that a new concert project has a 0.6 probability of earning a profit of N500,000 and a 0.4 probability of making a loss of N200,000. What is the expected value of the project?
questions.explanation: Expected value = sum of (probability x outcome) = 0.6 x 500,000 + 0.4 x (-200,000) = 300,000 - 80,000 = N220,000. Option D treats the loss as a gain and adds it. Option A takes a simple average and ignores the probabilities, and option C forgets the loss entirely.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A manager compares two investments. Investment P pays N800,000 with probability 0.5 or N200,000 with probability 0.5. Investment Q pays N600,000 with probability 0.7 or N300,000 with probability 0.3. Using expected value, which investment should be chosen and what is its expected value?

options.a: Investment P, with expected value N500,000
options.b: Investment Q, with expected value N450,000
options.c: Investment Q, with expected value N510,000
options.d: Investment P, because its highest payoff is N800,000

questions.explanation: EV(P) = 0.5 x 800,000 + 0.5 x 200,000 = N500,000; EV(Q) = 0.7 x 600,000 + 0.3 x 300,000 = N510,000, so Q is higher. Option D picks the investment with the biggest single payoff and ignores probabilities. Option B takes a simple average of Q's payoffs instead of weighting them.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A distributor in Onitsha estimates monthly profit from a new product line as follows: high demand N1,500,000 (probability 0.2), medium demand N900,000 (probability 0.5), low demand N400,000 (probability 0.3). What is the expected monthly profit?
questions.explanation: Expected profit = 0.2 x 1,500,000 + 0.5 x 900,000 + 0.3 x 400,000 = 300,000 + 450,000 + 120,000 = N870,000. Option C is a simple average that ignores probabilities. Option B just takes the most likely outcome, and option A leaves out the low-demand outcome.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A caterer must pay a fixed cost of N1,000,000 to serve at a wedding fair. Revenue will be N2,000,000 if attendance is high (probability 0.3) or N1,200,000 if attendance is low (probability 0.7). What is the expected PROFIT from attending the fair?
questions.explanation: Expected revenue = 0.3 x 2,000,000 + 0.7 x 1,200,000 = N1,440,000; expected profit = N1,440,000 - 1,000,000 = N440,000. Option D forgets to subtract the fixed cost. Option B uses a simple average of revenues, and option C uses only the low-attendance revenue.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A project has three possible outcomes: a gain of N400,000 (probability 0.25), a gain of N250,000 (probability 0.45), or a loss of N100,000. Only these three outcomes are possible. What is the expected value of the project?
questions.explanation: The probabilities must sum to 1, so P(loss) = 1 - 0.25 - 0.45 = 0.30; EV = 0.25 x 400,000 + 0.45 x 250,000 + 0.30 x (-100,000) = 100,000 + 112,500 - 30,000 = N182,500. Option C adds the loss instead of subtracting it. Option B ignores the loss outcome, and option A is a simple average.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Records show that a warehouse in Apapa has a 5% chance of a fire in any year, and a fire would cause a loss of N4,000,000. What is the expected annual loss from fire?
questions.explanation: Expected loss = probability x loss = 0.05 x 4,000,000 = N200,000. Option B uses 0.5 instead of 0.05, and option C uses 0.005, both errors in converting 5% to a decimal. Option A subtracts the expected loss from the full loss, which has no meaning.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A bag contains 100 balls: 40 red and 60 black. A player wins N1,000 if a red ball is drawn at random and nothing otherwise. What is the expected value of one draw?
questions.explanation: P(red) = 40/100 = 0.4, so EV = 0.4 x 1,000 + 0.6 x 0 = N400. Option A uses the probability of black instead of red. Option C wrongly assumes a 50-50 chance, and option D ignores probability altogether.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Supplier X charges N2,000,000; there is a 0.1 probability of late delivery, which would add N500,000 in extra costs. Supplier Y charges N1,950,000; there is a 0.4 probability of late delivery, which would add N400,000. Based on expected total cost, which supplier should be chosen?

options.d: Supplier Y, because its price is lower at N1,950,000

questions.explanation: Expected cost(X) = 2,000,000 + 0.1 x 500,000 = N2,050,000; expected cost(Y) = 1,950,000 + 0.4 x 400,000 = N2,110,000, so X is cheaper on average. Option D looks only at the quoted price and ignores the risk of late delivery. Option C adds the full late-delivery cost without weighting it by its probability.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A group decision-making technique in which members freely suggest as many ideas as possible while criticism of any idea is withheld until later is called
questions.explanation: Brainstorming encourages a free flow of many ideas and forbids criticism during idea generation, which supports creativity. Option D collects expert opinions anonymously through questionnaires without face-to-face meetings. Option C is a problem in groups, not a technique.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: In which group decision technique do experts who never meet face to face answer a series of questionnaires, with a coordinator summarising responses and sending them back until a consensus emerges?
questions.explanation: The Delphi technique uses anonymous experts, repeated questionnaire rounds and feedback from a coordinator, with no face-to-face meeting. Option B also uses independent idea writing, but members meet in the same room to present and vote. Option A is a face-to-face idea session.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: The nominal group technique is a group decision method in which members

options.a: argue openly until the most senior member decides
options.b: meet only online and never see one another's ideas
options.c: write ideas independently, present them one at a time, discuss them, then rank them individually
options.d: answer mailed questionnaires anonymously over several rounds

questions.explanation: In the nominal group technique members meet but first write their ideas silently, present them in turn, discuss them and then rank them independently, which stops a few loud members from dominating. Option D describes the Delphi technique. Option A is the kind of domination the technique is designed to prevent.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A situation in which pressure for agreement in a cohesive group causes members to suppress doubts and fail to examine alternatives critically is called
questions.explanation: Groupthink occurs when the desire for agreement overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives, so dissent is suppressed. Option D is a technique that deliberately encourages many ideas. Option C is members putting in less effort in a group, not suppressing disagreement.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: Which of the following is generally regarded as an ADVANTAGE of group decision-making over individual decision-making?

options.a: It brings more complete information and a wider range of alternatives
options.b: It is usually faster than an individual decision
options.c: It removes all pressure to conform
options.d: It makes responsibility for the outcome very clear

questions.explanation: Groups pool members' knowledge, so they bring more complete information and generate more alternatives, which also improves acceptance of the decision. Option B is wrong because groups are usually slower. Options D and C are actually disadvantages: responsibility becomes ambiguous and pressure to conform can increase.

questions.topic: Managerial Decision-Making and Problem Solving
questions.question: A Lagos bank's credit committee appoints one member to deliberately argue against every loan proposal before it is approved, so that weaknesses are exposed. This practice is meant mainly to reduce
questions.explanation: A devil's advocate challenges the group's preferred option, which forces critical examination and guards against groupthink. Option C is about accepting good-enough options, which the advocate does not target directly. Option D is wrong because criteria are still needed to judge proposals.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Organisational Behaviour draws on psychology, sociology, anthropology, economics and political science. This feature is described as its:
questions.explanation: Organisational Behaviour borrows ideas and methods from several disciplines, which is what inter-disciplinary means. Option B refers to its aim of improving organisational effectiveness and performance. Option C refers to the field evolving as organisations change, and option D refers to applying its principles to solve workplace problems.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: At which level of Organisational Behaviour would a study of employees' personality, perception and job satisfaction fall?
questions.explanation: Personality, perception, learning, motivation and job satisfaction are characteristics of individual people, so they belong to the individual level. Option C covers things like team dynamics, communication and conflict among people. Option A covers structure, culture and organisational change, and option D is not one of the three levels of Organisational Behaviour.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Organisational culture, organisational structure and organisational change are studied at which level of Organisational Behaviour?
questions.explanation: Culture, structure, change and development are properties of the organisation as a whole, so they belong to the organisational level. Option B covers personal traits like personality and perception. Option D covers teamwork and group decision-making, and option A is not one of the three levels.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The feature of Organisational Behaviour that means it relies on research and systematic analysis rather than assumption is its:
questions.explanation: Organisational Behaviour applies scientific methods, such as research and analysis, to study human behaviour at work. Option A refers to its focus on people and relationships. Options B and D refer to the field changing over time and to its aim of improving effectiveness.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A company sets up a committee to organise its end-of-year event. Once the event is over, the committee is dissolved. What type of group is this?
questions.explanation: A task group is a formal group created to complete a specific project or assignment, such as organising an event. Option B is also formal, but it consists of a manager and the subordinates who report directly to them. Options A and C are informal groups that form through social interaction, not by the organisation's design.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A group made up of a manager and the subordinates who report directly to that manager is called:
questions.explanation: A command group is set out by the organisation chart: a supervisor plus the people who report to them. Option A is formed for a specific project and crosses normal reporting lines. Options C and D are informal groups that arise from employees' own social ties and shared interests.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes informal groups from formal groups?

options.a: Informal groups always have a supervisor, while formal groups never do
options.b: Informal groups exist only outside the workplace
options.c: Informal groups are created by management, while formal groups arise from friendships
options.d: Informal groups develop naturally through social interaction among employees, while formal groups are deliberately established by the organisation

questions.explanation: Formal groups, such as command and task groups, are set up deliberately by the organisation, while informal groups, such as friendship and interest groups, grow out of social interaction. Option C reverses the two. Option A is wrong because informal groups have no officially appointed supervisor, and option B is wrong because informal groups form inside the workplace too.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: What is the correct order of the five stages of group development?
questions.explanation: Groups first come together (forming), then go through friction as opinions clash (storming), settle on norms and trust (norming), become productive (performing), and finally disband (adjourning). Options A, C and D each put at least one stage out of sequence; in particular, norming comes after storming, not before it.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: In which stage of group development do members express differing opinions and ideas, often causing friction?
questions.explanation: Storming is when members push their own views and the group experiences conflict as it finds its footing. Option A comes after this, when norms, trust and cooperation are established. Option B is when the group becomes fully functional, and option D is when it disbands.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A project team has completed its assignment and its members are being released back to their departments. Which stage of group development is this?
questions.explanation: Adjourning is the final stage, when the group disbands after its purpose has been fulfilled. Option C is the stage before, when the team is working productively. Options B and D are early stages, when the group first comes together and then agrees on norms.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The shared expectations that guide how members of a group are supposed to behave are called group:
questions.explanation: Norms are the agreed standards of behaviour that members are expected to follow, and they strongly shape how a group behaves. Option C is the number of members, which affects coordination and communication. Option D is the use of pressure or force on members, and option A is a stage of group development, not a factor shaping behaviour.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which group of items lists factors that influence group behaviour?

options.a: Group size, norms, leadership and communication

questions.explanation: Group size, norms, leadership and communication (along with coercion) all shape how a group actually behaves day to day. Option C lists stages of group development rather than influencing factors. Option D lists the functions of management, and option B lists the core elements of an organisation.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The field of study that examines how individuals, groups and organisational structures affect one another and behaviour within organisations is called
questions.explanation: Organisational behaviour studies how individuals, groups and organisational structures affect one another, so managers can understand and improve behaviour at work. Option B is forecasting staff needs. Option C is a planned change effort, which is one topic inside OB rather than the whole field.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Describing organisational behaviour as having a 'scientific approach' means that it

options.a: uses laboratory equipment to measure workers' physical strength
options.b: depends mainly on the personal opinions of managers
options.c: applies research and analysis to study human behaviour rather than relying on assumption
options.d: studies only machines and technology in the workplace

questions.explanation: OB applies scientific methods, relying on research and analysis rather than assumption, to understand people at work. Option B is the opposite, because opinion without evidence is what the scientific approach avoids. Options A and D confuse OB with physical or engineering studies.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Organisational behaviour is inter-disciplinary. Which of the following is NOT one of the disciplines it draws from?
questions.explanation: OB draws from psychology, sociology, anthropology, political science, economics and management, all of which study human behaviour or organisations. Civil engineering deals with structures such as roads and bridges, not human behaviour. Options C, D and B are core contributing disciplines.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The statement that organisational behaviour is 'goal oriented' means that its ultimate objective is to

options.b: improve organisational effectiveness and employee performance
options.c: increase the number of rules in the organisation
options.d: reduce the wages paid to employees

questions.explanation: Being goal oriented means OB aims to improve organisational effectiveness and employee performance. Option C confuses OB with bureaucracy. Options A and D are not aims of OB at all.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Organisational behaviour is described as a 'dynamic field' because it

options.a: deals with the movement of goods in a warehouse
options.b: has fixed principles that never change
options.c: studies only the behaviour of top managers
options.d: keeps evolving as organisations adapt to environmental and technological changes

questions.explanation: OB is dynamic because it evolves continuously as organisations adapt to changes in their environment and technology. Option B is the opposite of dynamic. Option A confuses OB with logistics.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: In the scope of organisational behaviour, perception, personality and job satisfaction are studied at which level?
questions.explanation: Perception, personality, learning, motivation, job satisfaction and emotion are individual-level topics because they concern each person. Option A covers topics like teamwork and group dynamics. Option D covers structure, culture and change.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Teamwork, power and politics, and conflict management fall under which level of organisational behaviour?
questions.explanation: These topics arise when people interact in groups, so they belong to the group level along with group dynamics, communication and leadership. Option C covers traits of single persons such as personality. Option A covers organisation-wide matters such as structure and culture.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the four elements of organisational behaviour?
questions.explanation: The four key elements of OB are people, structure, technology and environment, which together shape how work is done. Option C lists the functions of management. Option A lists stages of group development and option B lists factors of production.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually listed as an importance of studying organisational behaviour?

options.c: It guarantees that the organisation will never face competition

questions.explanation: OB helps improve performance, job satisfaction, leadership, communication, teamwork and change, and reduces conflict. No field of study can guarantee freedom from competition. Options B, D and A are all listed benefits.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: In organisational behaviour, a group is best defined as

options.a: a collection of individuals who interact, share common interests and goals, and work together to achieve an objective
options.b: a single employee working alone on a specialised task
options.c: any number of people who happen to be in the same place at the same time
options.d: all the customers who buy a company's product

questions.explanation: A group needs interaction, common goals and shared effort toward an objective. Option C describes a crowd, such as passengers at a bus stop, who do not interact toward a shared goal. Option B cannot be a group because a group needs two or more people.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a group?

options.b: Members work in complete isolation from one another

questions.explanation: Groups are marked by two or more people, common goals, interaction, mutual influence, shared norms and values, and interdependence. Working in complete isolation means no interaction, so it cannot describe a group. Options A, C and D are listed features.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A branch manager at a Nigerian bank and the five officers who report directly to her form a
questions.explanation: A command group is a formal group made up of a manager and the subordinates who report directly to that manager. Option A is a formal group formed for a specific project. Options D and B are informal groups that grow out of social ties rather than the reporting structure.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A company sets up a committee of staff from different departments to organise its 25th anniversary dinner, after which the committee will be dissolved. This committee is a
questions.explanation: A task group is a formal group formed to complete a specific project or assignment, such as a committee to organise a company event. Option D is a manager with direct subordinates. Options B and C are informal groups that form through social interaction, not management's design.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Several employees at an Ikeja factory who all support the same football club meet every Monday to discuss weekend matches. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Informal groups develop through social interaction among employees, such as interest and friendship groups, rather than being formed by management. Options D, B and A are all formal groups created by the organisation for work purposes.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: What is the main difference between formal and informal groups?

options.a: Informal groups exist only outside working hours
options.b: Formal groups have no leaders, while informal groups always do
options.c: Formal groups always have more members than informal groups
options.d: Formal groups are created by the organisation for work purposes; informal groups emerge from social interaction among employees

questions.explanation: Formal groups, such as command and task groups, are deliberately set up by the organisation, while informal groups such as friendship and interest groups arise naturally. Option C is wrong because size does not define the type. Option A is wrong because informal groups operate inside the workplace too.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
