questions.question: Members of a newly formed project team at a Lagos firm are polite but unsure of the team's purpose, structure and leadership. The team is in the
questions.explanation: Forming is the first stage, marked by uncertainty about purpose, structure and leadership while members get to know one another. Option A comes next, when members begin to express opinions and clash. Option D comes when the team becomes fully functional.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Members of a group begin to express their opinions and ideas openly, and disagreements arise over who should lead and how work should be done. This describes the
questions.explanation: In the storming stage members express opinions and ideas, and conflict over roles and leadership is common. Option C is the polite, uncertain start. Option D follows storming, when trust and norms are established.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The stage of group development in which members establish norms and strong relationships built on trust, cooperation and unity is the
questions.explanation: Norming is when the group agrees its norms and builds trust, cooperation and unity. Option C is the conflict stage that comes before it. Option B comes after, when the group is fully functional and focused on the task.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A task group set up to organise a company conference completes its work and is disbanded. It has reached the
questions.explanation: Adjourning is the final stage, when a temporary group wraps up and disbands. Option C is when the group is functioning well on its task. Option B is the start of a group's life, not its end.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The model of group development made up of forming, storming, norming and performing (with adjourning added later) is associated with
questions.explanation: Bruce Tuckman proposed forming, storming, norming and performing in 1965, and adjourning was added later with Mary Ann Jensen. Option B is known for bounded rationality. Option C is known for the three levels of organisational culture.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A department of 25 people finds that meetings drag on, not everyone gets a chance to speak, and coordination is difficult. Which factor influencing group behaviour is most clearly at work?
questions.explanation: Group size affects behaviour: as groups grow, coordination becomes harder and members get fewer chances to contribute. Option B involves force or threats, which is not described. Option D concerns accepted standards of behaviour, which are not the issue here.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Acceptable standards of behaviour that are shared by members of a group are called
questions.explanation: Norms are the shared standards of acceptable behaviour in a group, such as how hard to work or how to dress. Option B refers to the set of behaviours expected of a person in a particular position. Option C refers to a socially defined rank or position.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes a work team from a work group?

options.a: A group always has more members than a team
options.b: A team's coordinated effort produces performance greater than the sum of individual inputs, while a group mainly shares information
options.c: A team has no leader, while a group always has one
options.d: A group has collective accountability, while a team has only individual accountability

questions.explanation: A work team creates positive synergy through coordinated effort and complementary skills, while a work group interacts mainly to share information and help each member perform in his own area. Option D reverses the accountability point: teams add mutual accountability. Option A is wrong because size does not distinguish them.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The tendency for individuals to put in less effort when working collectively than when working alone is called
questions.explanation: Social loafing happens when people in a group reduce effort because individual contributions are hard to identify. Option B is the suppression of dissent for the sake of agreement. Option D is the opposite effect, where combined effort exceeds the sum of individual inputs.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The degree to which group members are attracted to one another and motivated to stay in the group is called
questions.explanation: Cohesiveness is how strongly members are attracted to each other and want to remain part of the group. Option A is uncertainty about what one's role requires. Option C is reduced effort in a group.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: In organisational behaviour, perception is best defined as the process by which individuals

options.a: form groups to achieve common objectives
options.b: organise and interpret sensory impressions to give meaning to their environment
options.c: copy the behaviour of their supervisors
options.d: transmit messages to other members of the organisation

questions.explanation: Perception is how people organise and interpret what their senses pick up, which is why two people can see the same event differently. Option C is a form of learning by imitation. Option D describes communication.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Factors that influence perception are usually grouped as factors in the perceiver, in the target and in the situation. Which of the following is NOT one of these three groups?
questions.explanation: Perception is shaped by the perceiver (attitudes, motives, experience), the target being perceived and the situation (time, setting). Shareholders are not one of these categories. Options A, D and C are the three standard groups.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A manager rates a new staff member highly on every aspect of performance simply because she is very articulate in meetings. This perceptual error is called
questions.explanation: The halo effect occurs when one positive characteristic shapes a general impression of a person. Option B is judging someone by the group he belongs to. Option C is judging someone by comparison with others encountered just before.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A recruiter assumes that a job applicant from a particular ethnic group must be good at trading, without assessing her individually. This is
questions.explanation: Stereotyping is judging a person on the basis of one's perception of the group to which that person belongs. Option B is letting one trait of the individual colour the whole impression. Option D is noticing only information consistent with one's interests.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: When his team meets its target, a supervisor says it was due to his excellent leadership; when the team misses its target, he blames poor market conditions. This shows
questions.explanation: Self-serving bias is attributing one's own successes to internal factors and failures to external factors. Option C is about judging OTHER people, overestimating internal causes of their behaviour. Option A is a decision bias about over-relying on first information.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: When judging the behaviour of others, the tendency to underestimate external factors and overestimate internal or personal factors is called
questions.explanation: The fundamental attribution error is blaming others' behaviour on their personality while overlooking the situation, for example assuming a late colleague is lazy when traffic was the cause. Option C concerns how people explain their OWN successes and failures. Option A is noticing selectively based on one's interests.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: In attribution theory, if a staff member has submitted every report late for the past year, his behaviour shows high
questions.explanation: Consistency asks whether the person responds the same way over time; late reports every month for a year is highly consistent, which points to an internal cause. Option A would mean he behaves differently across situations. Option C would mean most colleagues also submit late.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Evaluative statements, favourable or unfavourable, about objects, people or events are called
questions.explanation: Attitudes are evaluative statements that reflect how a person feels about something, such as 'I like my job'. Option B is the process of interpreting sensory impressions. Option C refers to shared group standards of behaviour.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The statement 'I am angry that my salary is lower than my colleague's' reflects which component of an attitude?
questions.explanation: The affective component is the emotional or feeling part of an attitude, here anger. Option D would be the belief itself, such as 'my salary is lower than his'. Option A would be the intention to act, such as 'I will look for another job'.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The statement 'I intend to resign and look for another job' reflects which component of an attitude?
questions.explanation: The behavioural component is the intention to behave in a certain way toward someone or something. Option B is a belief or opinion and option D is the feeling attached to it.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: The discomfort a person feels when there is incompatibility between two or more attitudes, or between behaviour and attitudes, is known as
questions.explanation: Cognitive dissonance is the tension felt when attitudes and behaviour do not match, for example a manager who values honesty being told to hide a product defect. People usually try to reduce it by changing an attitude or behaviour. Option D is unclear role expectations and option C is reduced effort in groups.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the 'Big Five' personality dimensions?
questions.explanation: The Big Five dimensions are extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability and openness to experience. Option A is a mental ability, not a personality dimension. Options B and D are a single behaviour and a job position respectively.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: In which small-group communication network does all information pass through one central person, so that a leader emerges clearly?
questions.explanation: In the wheel network a central figure acts as the conduit for all group communication, so the network is centralised, fast and leader-focused. Option D lets every member communicate with every other member. Option C links each member only to the two people beside him.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A communication network in which every member of a team can communicate directly with every other member is called the
questions.explanation: In the all-channel network everyone communicates freely with everyone else, which is typical of self-managed teams. Option B routes everything through one central person. Option C follows the formal chain of command step by step.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A message that passes from the managing director to the general manager, then to a department head and then to a supervisor, following the formal line of authority, is moving through which network?
questions.explanation: The chain network rigidly follows the formal chain of command, passing information level by level. Option A would have one central person speaking directly with every member. Option D would let every member talk to every other member.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Of the chain, wheel and all-channel communication networks, which is generally associated with the HIGHEST member satisfaction?

options.b: All three give the same level of satisfaction

questions.explanation: The all-channel network gives every member an equal chance to participate, so it is associated with high member satisfaction. Option A centralises communication in one person, which lowers satisfaction for everyone else. Option C restricts members to passing messages along a fixed line.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which of the following is a barrier to effective communication in organisations?
questions.explanation: Information overload occurs when the information people receive exceeds their capacity to process it, so messages are ignored or forgotten. Options B, A and D are ways to improve communication, not barriers to it.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: A sales officer reports only the good news to his regional manager and leaves out falling sales figures so that he looks good. This barrier to communication is called
questions.explanation: Filtering is a sender's deliberate manipulation of information so the receiver sees it more favourably. Option D is receiving more information than one can process. Option B is the normal step where the receiver interprets a message.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: In conflict management, a style that is high in both assertiveness and cooperativeness, where parties work together to find a solution that fully satisfies everyone, is called
questions.explanation: Collaborating seeks a win-win outcome that fully meets both parties' concerns, so it is high on both assertiveness and cooperativeness. Option C is a middle position where each side gives up something. Option D puts the other party's concerns above one's own.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Two managers at a Lagos firm each want the whole of a N10 million training budget. They agree that each will get N5 million, so each gives up part of what he wanted. This conflict-handling style is
questions.explanation: Compromising means each party gives up something to reach a middle position, as with splitting the budget. Option C would look for a solution that satisfies both fully, for example finding extra funds. Option A means one side pushes to win at the other's expense.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Conflict that supports the goals of a group and improves its performance is called
questions.explanation: Functional conflict is constructive: it supports group goals, for example a debate that exposes a weak plan. Option B hinders group performance. Option A focuses on personal relationships and is usually harmful.

questions.topic: Organisational Behaviour, Communication and Team Dynamics
questions.question: Which of the following is listed as an importance of groups in an organisation?

options.a: They guarantee that conflict never occurs
options.b: They enhance problem solving and improve decision making
options.c: They remove the need for managers
options.d: They allow individuals to avoid all responsibility

questions.explanation: Groups facilitate communication, promote cooperation, improve decision making, enhance problem solving and increase motivation. Option C is wrong because groups still need leadership. Options A and D are false; groups can create conflict and do not remove responsibility.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: In the Competing Values Framework, which culture type combines an internal focus with flexibility and emphasises teamwork, relationships and mentoring?
questions.explanation: Clan culture is internally focused and flexible, like an extended family built on collaboration and mentoring. Option C is also flexible but externally focused on innovation and risk-taking. Options A and D emphasise stability and control, with market culture focused on results and hierarchy culture on processes and efficiency.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A fast-moving software start-up that values innovation, risk-taking and entrepreneurship most closely fits which culture type in the Competing Values Framework?
questions.explanation: Adhocracy culture is externally focused and flexible, prizing creativity, experimentation and entrepreneurship. Option C values stability, rules and careful processes, which is the opposite. Option D focuses on internal relationships, and option A focuses on competing and delivering results through control.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A government agency that emphasises formal procedures, efficiency, cost control and careful, rule-based decision-making best illustrates which culture type?
questions.explanation: Hierarchy culture combines an internal focus with stability and control, giving a structured, procedure-driven workplace. Option C values innovation and flexibility. Option A values relationships and teamwork, and option D, though also control-oriented, looks outward to competition and results.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: The two dimensions used in the Competing Values Framework to classify organisational culture are:

options.a: Internal versus external focus, and flexibility versus stability (control)
options.b: Tall versus flat structure, and centralised versus decentralised authority
options.c: Profit versus non-profit, and public versus private ownership
options.d: Strong versus weak culture, and formal versus informal structure

questions.explanation: The framework crosses an internal-external focus axis with a flexibility-stability axis to produce the clan, adhocracy, market and hierarchy cultures. Options B, C and D describe other ways of classifying organisations, not the axes of this framework.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Colleagues follow a manager's advice because she is the only person in the firm who fully understands its new accounting software. Which base of power does she have?
questions.explanation: Expert power comes from having specialised knowledge or skills that others need. Option C comes from holding a formal position. Option D comes from being admired or liked so that others want to identify with the person, and option A comes from the ability to punish.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A supervisor gets compliance by threatening to deny workers overtime or issue queries. Which base of power is being used?
questions.explanation: Coercive power rests on the belief that a person can punish or withhold something valued. Option D is the opposite, based on granting desired outcomes like bonuses or recognition. Options A and B rest on knowledge and on personal attraction, not on threats.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Employees accept a new head of department's instructions simply because of the official position she has been appointed to. This is:
questions.explanation: Legitimate power is based on the belief that a person has the right to influence others because of their position or role. Option C comes from personal admiration, and option A from specialised knowledge. Option B depends on the ability to give rewards, which is not what makes employees follow her here.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which base of power is based on others admiring a person and wanting to identify with or be accepted by them?
questions.explanation: Referent power flows from personal charisma and the desire of others to associate with the person. Option D comes from formal authority. Options A and C come from the ability to punish or to reward.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes the informal organisation from the formal organisation?

options.a: The informal organisation consists only of written policies and procedures
options.b: The informal organisation is shown on the organisation chart, while the formal organisation is not
options.c: The informal organisation is easier for management to control than the formal organisation
options.d: The informal organisation is the unofficial network of relationships that emerges naturally, while the formal organisation is the structure deliberately designed by management

questions.explanation: The formal organisation is the official design of roles, reporting lines and channels, while the informal organisation is the network of personal relationships that grows as people interact. Options A and B describe features of the formal organisation. Option C is wrong because the informal organisation is harder, not easier, to control.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A department's official reporting lines run through its manager, but staff actually turn to a long-serving colleague for advice and news. This colleague's influence is part of the:
questions.explanation: Influence that arises from personal relationships and trust rather than official position belongs to the informal organisation, which shows how the organisation actually works. Options A, B and D all refer to the official, designed structure that shows how the organisation is supposed to work.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: The pattern of shared values, beliefs, assumptions and norms that shapes how members of an organisation think and behave is called
questions.explanation: Organisational culture is the shared system of values, beliefs and assumptions that guides how people behave at work, often summed up as 'the way we do things here'. Option A is the formal arrangement of roles and reporting lines. Option D is only a diagram of that structure.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Organisational culture matters mainly because it

options.a: shapes employee beliefs, behaviours and working relationships, and affects how well the organisation adapts
options.b: fixes the salaries of all employees
options.c: replaces the need for formal rules and structure
options.d: applies only to employees at the top of the hierarchy

questions.explanation: Culture shapes employees' beliefs, behaviours and working relationships, and can help or hinder the organisation's ability to adapt to its external environment. Option C overstates it; culture works alongside structure rather than replacing it. Option D is wrong because culture affects everyone in the organisation.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: The model that describes organisational culture at three levels - artifacts, espoused values and basic underlying assumptions - was developed by
questions.explanation: Edgar Schein described culture as having three levels, from visible artifacts to espoused values to deeply held basic assumptions. Option A is known for the stages of group development. Option B is known for the power, role, task and person cultures.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which option arranges Schein's levels of organisational culture from the MOST visible to the LEAST visible?

options.a: Artifacts, basic underlying assumptions, espoused values
options.b: Basic underlying assumptions, espoused values, artifacts
options.c: Artifacts, espoused values, basic underlying assumptions
options.d: Espoused values, artifacts, basic underlying assumptions

questions.explanation: Artifacts are the visible surface, espoused values are the stated beliefs below them, and basic underlying assumptions are the deepest, unconscious level. Option B gives the order from least to most visible. Options D and A mix up the middle and surface levels.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Visitors to a Lagos tech start-up notice open-plan offices, staff in jeans and colourful murals on the walls. In Schein's model, these are examples of
questions.explanation: Artifacts are the visible, tangible parts of culture such as office layout, dress, logos and ceremonies. Option D refers to the values the company states, for example in a mission statement. Option C is the deepest, taken-for-granted level that visitors cannot see.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A bank's published code of conduct declares that 'integrity, customer focus and teamwork' are its core values. In Schein's model, these stated values belong to the level of
questions.explanation: Espoused values are the strategies, goals and values an organisation openly states and claims to hold. Option B refers to visible items such as buildings, dress and logos. Option C refers to beliefs so deeply held they are taken for granted and rarely stated.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: In Schein's model, basic underlying assumptions are

options.a: the logos, uniforms and office designs of the organisation
options.b: the formal rules found in the staff handbook
options.c: deeply held, taken-for-granted beliefs that are often unconscious and hard to change
options.d: the values written in the company's annual report

questions.explanation: Basic underlying assumptions are the deepest level of culture: beliefs so taken for granted that people rarely question or even notice them, which makes them hard to change. Option A describes artifacts. Option D describes espoused values.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A strong organisational culture is one in which

options.a: the core values are intensely held and widely shared by members
options.c: the rules are written down in great detail
options.d: there are many conflicting subcultures and no shared values

questions.explanation: In a strong culture the organisation's core values are both intensely held and widely shared, so they have a big influence on behaviour. Option D describes a weak culture. Option C is about formalisation, which is different from cultural strength.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which of the following is generally associated with a STRONG organisational culture?

options.a: The absence of any shared values
options.b: Weak influence of shared values on employee behaviour
options.c: Constant disagreement about what the organisation stands for
options.d: Lower employee turnover, because staff agree on what the organisation stands for

questions.explanation: Because members share and commit to the same core values, a strong culture builds loyalty and is linked with lower employee turnover. Options C, B and A all describe a weak culture, in which values are not widely shared.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A possible DISADVANTAGE of a very strong organisational culture is that it can

options.a: make employees unsure of the organisation's values
options.b: become a barrier to change when the environment shifts
options.c: cause staff to have no loyalty to the organisation

questions.explanation: Strong cultures make people cling to established ways, so they can become a barrier to change, diversity and mergers when conditions change. Options A, D and C describe problems of weak cultures, not strong ones.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: The core values shared by a majority of an organisation's members, as opposed to values found only in particular departments, are called the
questions.explanation: The dominant culture expresses the core values shared by most members and gives the organisation its distinct personality. Option D is a mini-culture within a department or location. Option C is the network of unofficial relationships, not a set of values.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Within a large Nigerian bank, the IT department has its own relaxed dress code and working style, while still sharing the bank's core values. The IT department has its own

options.c: basic underlying assumptions for the whole bank

questions.explanation: A subculture is a mini-culture within part of an organisation, reflecting that unit's common problems or experiences, while keeping the core values. Option D refers to the values shared across most of the bank. Option A refers to the officially designed structure.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common way employees learn an organisation's culture?

options.a: Material symbols and the organisation's special language
options.b: Stories about the founder and past events

questions.explanation: Culture is passed on through stories, rituals, physical symbols (such as office layout or company cars) and language specific to the organisation. The national constitution is a legal document of a country, not a carrier of a particular company's culture. Options B, D and A are standard ways culture is transmitted.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the four culture types in the Competing Values Framework?
questions.explanation: The Competing Values Framework identifies clan, adhocracy, hierarchy and market cultures. Option C is Charles Handy's classification of culture, a different model. Option A mixes terms about cultural strength and subcultures.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A culture with an external focus and flexibility that emphasises innovation, risk-taking and entrepreneurship is the
questions.explanation: The adhocracy culture faces outward and stays flexible, encouraging innovation, risk-taking and entrepreneurship, as in software or film. Option C is flexible but internally focused on relationships. Option D is external but focused on results and competition rather than innovation.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A culture with an internal focus and stability that emphasises efficiency, process, cost control and careful decision-making is the
questions.explanation: The hierarchy culture is internally focused and controlled, emphasising efficiency, process, cost control and careful decision-making, which suits bureaucratic organisations. Option C is externally focused on competition and results. Option D is internal but flexible and people-centred.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A culture with an external focus and stability that concentrates on competing, delivering results, speed and getting things done is the
questions.explanation: The market culture is externally focused and controlled, driving competition, results and speed, which suits sales-and-delivery-driven organisations. Option D shares the stability but looks inward at process. Option A shares the external focus but values flexibility and innovation.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A young Lagos animation studio rewards staff for experimenting with new ideas, accepts failures as part of learning and constantly launches new products. Its culture is best described as
questions.explanation: Innovation, experimentation and risk-taking with an outward focus are the marks of an adhocracy culture, common in fast-paced creative industries. Option B would stress rules, process and cost control. Option A would stress beating competitors and hitting sales targets.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A government parastatal in Abuja runs on detailed procedures, multiple approval levels and strict cost control, and staff are rewarded for following process carefully. Its culture is best described as
questions.explanation: An internal focus on process, efficiency, cost control and careful decisions is the hierarchy culture, typical of bureaucratic organisations. Option D would favour risk-taking and innovation. Option A would emphasise winning customers and results speed over procedure.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A Nigerian beverage distributor ranks its sales teams weekly, pays large bonuses for beating targets and talks constantly about taking market share from rivals. Its culture is best described as
questions.explanation: An external, results-driven focus on competing, hitting targets and speed is the market culture. Option B would put relationships and mentoring first. Option A would focus inward on process and rules rather than beating rivals.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: In Charles Handy's classification of culture, a culture in which power is concentrated in one central figure, often the founder, and is pictured as a spider's web is the
questions.explanation: Handy's power culture radiates from a central person, like a spider at the centre of a web, which is common in small owner-managed firms. Option C is based on rules, procedures and job roles. Option A is built around project teams and expertise.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: In Handy's classification, a culture built on clearly defined job roles, rules and procedures, typical of large bureaucracies and civil services, is the
questions.explanation: The role culture relies on formal roles, rules and procedures, and power comes from one's position; Handy pictured it as a Greek temple. Option A centres on one powerful person. Option B organises work around project teams.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: In organisational behaviour, power is best defined as

options.a: the formal job title a person holds
options.b: the total number of subordinates a manager supervises
options.c: the capacity of one person to influence the behaviour of another
options.d: the amount of money a person earns

questions.explanation: Power is the capacity to influence the behaviour of others, so that they act in ways they otherwise would not. Option A is only one possible basis of power, legitimate position. Options B and D may be linked to power but do not define it.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: The typology of five bases of power - reward, coercive, legitimate, expert and referent - was developed by
questions.explanation: John French and Bertram Raven identified the five bases of social power. Option A is linked to the stages of group development. Option C is linked to the Competing Values Framework of culture.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of French and Raven's five bases of power?
questions.explanation: French and Raven's five bases are reward, coercive, referent, expert and legitimate power. Charisma is usually discussed under referent power, but 'charismatic power' is not one of the five named bases. Options C, D and B are all in the typology.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Power based on the belief that a person can grant desired outcomes such as money or recognition is called
questions.explanation: Reward power rests on the ability to give things people value, such as pay rises, bonuses or recognition. Option B is the opposite, the ability to punish. Option A rests on the right that comes with a position.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Power based on the belief that a person can punish others, by inflicting harm or withholding something they value, is called
questions.explanation: Coercive power depends on fear of punishment, such as a query, demotion or withheld bonus. Option A depends on granting desired outcomes. Option D depends on specialised knowledge.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Power based on the belief that a person has the 'right' to influence others by virtue of their position or role is called
questions.explanation: Legitimate power comes from a formal position, so subordinates accept that the holder has the right to give instructions. Option D comes from others admiring and wanting to identify with the person. Option A comes from specialised knowledge.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Staff at a Lagos hospital follow the advice of a junior IT officer on cybersecurity because she is the only one who understands the new system. She is using
questions.explanation: Expert power is based on the belief that a person has, and is willing to share, needed knowledge, regardless of rank. Option A would require a senior position, which she does not hold. Options B and D involve punishing or rewarding, which she cannot do.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Young employees at a Nigerian media company copy the dress and work habits of a popular, admired colleague and want to be accepted by her, although she has no formal authority over them. Her influence comes from
questions.explanation: Referent power is based on others wanting to associate with or be accepted by a person they admire. Option D requires formal position, which she lacks. Option C would require specialised knowledge to be the reason they follow her.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: A factory supervisor in Agbara tells workers that anyone who arrives late will lose a day's pay. The supervisor is relying mainly on
questions.explanation: Threatening to withhold pay is a form of punishment, so the supervisor is using coercive power. Option D would involve offering something desirable for good behaviour. Option B depends on admiration rather than threats.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which bases of power tend to produce GENUINE COMMITMENT from followers?
questions.explanation: Referent and expert power come from the person rather than the position, and they tend to produce genuine commitment. Reward and legitimate power produce mixed results, while coercive power often brings mere compliance with resentment. So options B, A and C all include bases that do not reliably produce commitment.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Heavy reliance on coercive power by a manager is most likely to result in

options.a: higher job satisfaction across the team
options.b: admiration and a desire to imitate the manager
options.c: mere compliance along with resentment and resistance

questions.explanation: Coercive power often produces only compliance, and it breeds resentment and resistance. Option D is the typical result of referent or expert power. Option B describes the basis of referent power, not a result of threats.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Of French and Raven's bases, which two are usually classed as PERSONAL power, coming from the individual rather than from the position held?
questions.explanation: Expert and referent power come from a person's own knowledge or attractiveness, so they move with the person if he changes jobs. Legitimate, reward and coercive power come from the formal position, so options C, D and B are positional (formal) power.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Political behaviour in organisations is best described as activities that

options.a: follow the official chain of command at all times
options.b: are not part of one's formal role but influence, or try to influence, the distribution of advantages and disadvantages
options.c: involve campaigning for national elections during office hours
options.d: are required by the job description and approved by management

questions.explanation: Organisational politics covers actions outside one's formal role used to gain or protect advantages, such as forming alliances or controlling information. Option D describes normal job duties. Option C confuses workplace politics with party politics.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of LEGITIMATE rather than illegitimate political behaviour?

options.a: Forming a coalition with colleagues to support a budget proposal
options.b: Hiding files that a co-worker needs
options.d: Spreading false rumours about a colleague

questions.explanation: Legitimate political behaviour is everyday politicking such as forming coalitions, lobbying or complaining to a supervisor. Options C, D and B are illegitimate because they violate the implied rules of the game and harm others.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which of the following organisational conditions is most likely to INCREASE political behaviour?

options.a: Scarce resources and unclear performance evaluation
options.c: High trust and objective performance measures
options.d: Clear roles and transparent reward systems

questions.explanation: Politics grows when resources are scarce, goals or roles are ambiguous and performance evaluation is unclear, because people compete for advantage. Options B, C and D describe conditions that reduce the need for political behaviour.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: The process by which individuals attempt to control the impression others form of them is called
questions.explanation: Impression management covers tactics such as flattery, self-promotion and conforming to opinions to shape how others see you. Option B is a perceiver's error, not something the target does. Option C is reduced effort in groups.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Before a promotion exercise, an officer in a Lagos firm repeatedly praises his manager's ideas and agrees with everything she says to win her favour. This political tactic is
questions.explanation: Ingratiation is using flattery, praise or friendliness to win favour before making a request. Option B involves enlisting others' support. Option C relies on logical arguments and facts.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: The formal organisation is best described as

options.a: the officially designed structure of roles, reporting lines and communication channels set up by management
options.b: the social clubs employees join after work
options.c: the grapevine through which rumours spread
options.d: the network of friendships that forms naturally among employees

questions.explanation: The formal organisation is what management deliberately designs: roles, reporting lines and official channels. Options D, C and B are all parts of the informal organisation, which emerges naturally.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: Which statement best captures the relationship between the formal and the informal organisation?

options.a: The informal organisation only hinders work and should be abolished
options.b: The formal organisation shows how the organisation is supposed to function; the informal organisation shows how it actually functions
options.c: The informal organisation is designed by management; the formal one emerges naturally
options.d: The two are identical in every organisation

questions.explanation: The formal organisation is designed and describes how work is supposed to happen, while the informal organisation emerges from daily relationships and reflects how work actually gets done. Option C reverses the two. Option A is wrong because the informal organisation can help as well as hinder work.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: In a Nigerian manufacturing firm, staff often go to a long-serving storekeeper, not their supervisors, to find out how to get things done quickly, through his network of friends across departments. This shows the influence of the
questions.explanation: The storekeeper's influence comes from unofficial relationships that emerged over time, which is the informal organisation at work. Option D would route requests through official reporting lines. Option A is wrong because his position gives him no formal authority over these staff.

questions.topic: Organisational Culture, Power and Politics
questions.question: In workplace diversity, which of the following is an example of DEEP-LEVEL diversity?

options.d: Differences in values, personality and work preferences

questions.explanation: Deep-level diversity refers to differences in values, personality and work preferences, which become clear only as people get to know each other. Options A, B and C are surface-level diversity, which is visible or easily known demographic differences.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: In the communication process, converting an idea into words, symbols or images is called:
questions.explanation: Encoding is the sender's job of turning an intended meaning into a form that can be transmitted. Option B is the reverse, when the receiver interprets the message. Option A is the receiver's response, and option D is anything that distorts or interferes with the message.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which sequence correctly represents the seven-part communication process?

options.a: Sender, Channel, Encoding, Message, Feedback, Receiver, Decoding
options.b: Receiver, Decoding, Message, Channel, Sender, Encoding, Feedback
options.c: Sender, Encoding, Message, Channel, Receiver, Decoding, Feedback
options.d: Sender, Message, Decoding, Channel, Receiver, Encoding, Feedback

questions.explanation: The sender encodes an idea into a message, sends it through a channel to the receiver, who decodes it and responds with feedback. Option D places decoding before the message reaches the receiver and encoding at the receiver's end. Options A and B also scramble the order, for example by starting with the receiver or giving feedback before decoding.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: In the communication process, anything that distorts, filters or interferes with accurate communication is called:
questions.explanation: Noise is any interference, such as jargon, distractions or bias, that causes the message to be misunderstood, and the sender should try to minimise it. Option B is the medium used, such as email or a meeting. Option D is the receiver's response, and option A is turning ideas into symbols.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which element of the communication process tells the sender whether the message was understood as intended?
questions.explanation: Feedback is the receiver's verbal or non-verbal response, and it confirms whether communication actually took place. Option A happens at the sender's end before transmission. Options B and D are the medium and the content, neither of which shows whether the message was understood.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Employees send complaints, reports and suggestions to their managers. This flow of formal communication is called:
questions.explanation: Upward communication flows from lower levels to higher levels of the organisation, carrying feedback, reports, complaints and suggestions. Option D flows from managers to subordinates, such as policies and instructions. Option A is between people at the same level, and option C is informal rather than formal.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A sales officer communicates directly with the head of the finance department, a different department and a higher level, outside the normal reporting line. This is:
questions.explanation: Diagonal communication cuts across both departments and hierarchical levels, outside the standard reporting structure. Option C is between people at the same level. Options A and B move up or down within the same chain of command.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: The informal communication network through which information spreads within an organisation outside official channels is called:
questions.explanation: The grapevine is the unofficial network of conversations and social contacts through which information travels at work. Option B is a formal channel. Options C and D represent official structures and documents, which are formal by definition.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the grapevine from a rumour?

options.a: The grapevine is the informal channel itself, while a rumour is unverified or distorted information that may travel through it
options.b: There is no difference; the two terms mean the same thing
options.c: The grapevine is a formal channel, while a rumour is an informal one
options.d: The grapevine always carries false information, while a rumour is always true

questions.explanation: The grapevine is the network, and true, false or partial information can pass through it; a rumour is specifically unverified or distorted information. Option D is wrong because grapevine information is not necessarily inaccurate and can even be faster than formal channels. Option C wrongly calls the grapevine formal, and option B ignores the difference between a channel and its content.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A manager sends a very short memo that leaves out the deadline staff need in order to act. Which characteristic of effective communication has been violated?
questions.explanation: A complete message gives the receiver enough information to understand and act on it, and missing the deadline breaks that rule. Option D is tempting, but conciseness means avoiding unnecessary information, not leaving out essential information. Options B and C relate to sending information while still useful and suiting tone and medium to the audience.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Information about a training session reaches employees the day after the session has taken place. Which characteristic of effective communication is missing?
questions.explanation: Timely communication arrives while the information is still useful, and a notice received after the event is useless. Option D is about factual correctness, which may still be fine here. Options A and C are about being easily understood and avoiding unnecessary detail.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Using language, tone and medium suited to the audience is which characteristic of effective communication?
questions.explanation: An appropriate message fits its audience, for example avoiding jargon with non-specialists or choosing a formal tone for official matters. Option B concerns facts being correct. Options A and D concern giving enough information and delivering it in time.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Business communication is best defined as:

options.b: Informal conversations among friends at work only
options.c: The systematic exchange of information, ideas, instructions and opinions among people within and outside an organisation to achieve its objectives
options.d: Communication among managers alone, excluding employees

questions.explanation: Business communication covers every exchange of information inside the organisation and with outsiders such as customers, suppliers, regulators and investors, all aimed at its goals. Option A is only one narrow form of external communication, option D leaves out employees, and option B covers only the informal grapevine.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A poor internet connection during an online meeting, a loud environment and language barriers are all examples of which element of communication?
questions.explanation: Noise is anything that interferes with accurate communication, whether physical (sound, bad network) or semantic (language). Option D is the receiver's response, option C is forming the message, and option A is the medium itself, such as email or a meeting.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: The receiver's response that shows the sender whether the message was understood is called:
questions.explanation: Feedback, such as an employee replying 'Yes, I understand the instructions', completes the process and tells the sender whether communication really happened. Option B is the receiver interpreting the message, option C is the sender forming it, and option A is the medium used to send it.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: The grapevine refers to:

options.a: The informal, unofficial communication network through which information spreads in an organisation
options.b: A formal written report sent to top management
options.c: The official chain of command used for formal instructions

questions.explanation: The grapevine is the informal network - chats between colleagues, office WhatsApp groups, lunch talk - that carries information outside official channels. Options C and B are formal communication, and option D is external communication.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which is a characteristic of formal communication?

options.b: It follows the official organisational structure and is usually documented
options.c: It is unofficial and usually leaves no records
options.d: It does not follow any hierarchy

questions.explanation: Formal communication moves through official channels and hierarchy, and it is usually recorded, such as memos, reports and official emails. Options C, A and D describe informal communication (the grapevine).

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: An employee sends a written complaint with suggestions to her head of department. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Upward communication flows from employees to management, carrying complaints, suggestions, feedback and reports. Option C flows from management to staff, option B is between people at the same level, and option D is informal, while this complaint is formal.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Communication between the marketing manager and the finance manager, who are at the same level in the organisation, is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal communication takes place between people or departments at the same level and helps coordination and teamwork. Options A and B move between levels in the hierarchy, and option C crosses both departments and levels, such as an HR manager speaking directly with a sales officer.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A Management Information System (MIS) is best described as:

options.a: A system, usually computer-based, that collects, processes, stores and provides information to managers for planning, decision-making and control
options.b: A machine used only for typing letters
options.c: The department that handles employee welfare
options.d: A system used only to process customer cash withdrawals

questions.explanation: An MIS turns raw data into useful information and delivers it to managers so they can plan, decide, coordinate and control. Option B is a single office tool, option C is an HR function, and option D describes one routine transaction, which is the work of a transaction processing system.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an importance of MIS?

options.a: It removes the need for managers to make decisions
options.b: It helps managers monitor and control performance
options.d: It supports better and faster decision-making

questions.explanation: An MIS supports managers' decisions with accurate, timely information; it does not replace managerial judgement. Options D, C and B are genuine benefits, along with better planning, productivity and customer service.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: An information system that processes routine daily business transactions such as payroll, sales and ATM transactions is called a:
questions.explanation: A TPS handles the high volume of everyday transactions that keep a business running. Option A gives summary information to top executives, option B helps managers with complex decisions, and option C supports office work such as word processing and email.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which of the following best describes data?

options.a: Facts that have been processed and organised for decision-making
options.b: Raw, unprocessed facts and figures with little meaning on their own
options.c: The final decision taken by management
options.d: Conclusions drawn by managers from reports

questions.explanation: Data are raw facts - such as daily sales figures or attendance records - that mean little until they are organised and analysed. Option A describes information, option D is an interpretation built on information, and option C is the result of the decision-making process.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A shop records sales of 250, 320 and 280 units on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. A manager's report then states: 'Sales rose by 28% from Monday to Tuesday, then fell slightly on Wednesday.' Which statement is correct?

options.a: Both the figures and the statement are information
options.b: The daily figures are data; the report's statement is information
options.c: Both the figures and the statement are data
options.d: The daily figures are information; the report's statement is data

questions.explanation: The three daily figures are raw facts (data), while the report processes them into a meaningful trend (information) that managers can act on; 320 is 28% more than 250. Option D reverses the two ideas, and options C and A ignore the difference between unprocessed input and processed output.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of good information?

options.a: It includes as much detail as possible, whether relevant or not
options.c: It is accurate, relevant and timely
options.d: It arrives after the decision has already been made

questions.explanation: Good information must be accurate, relevant and timely, as well as complete, reliable and understandable. Option B describes data, option D is useless because it comes too late, and option A leads to information overload.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Digital communication is:

options.a: The exchange of information using electronic devices and digital technologies such as email, video conferencing and messaging apps
options.d: Communication only through printed letters and memos

questions.explanation: Digital communication uses the internet and electronic systems, such as email, WhatsApp, Zoom or Teams, to send and receive information quickly. Option D is traditional written communication, option C is oral communication, and option B is non-verbal communication.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which is an ADVANTAGE of digital communication?

options.a: Speed and lower cost, since messages arrive instantly with less spending on paper, postage and transport
options.b: Dependence on internet access and power supply

questions.explanation: Digital tools deliver messages instantly and cut the costs of paper, postage and travel, which is why firms rely on them. Options D, B and C are disadvantages or challenges of digital communication.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which of the following is a CHALLENGE of digital communication for many Nigerian organisations?

options.a: Poor internet connectivity and power outages
options.b: Faster collaboration among staff in different locations

questions.explanation: Digital communication depends on stable internet and electricity, so poor connectivity and power outages are real challenges. Options D, C and B are advantages of digital communication, not problems.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Remote work (telecommuting) means:

options.a: Employees performing their duties outside the traditional office using digital communication technologies
options.b: Contracting all of a firm's work out to another company
options.d: Employees working only at the head office

questions.explanation: Remote work lets employees do their jobs from home, co-working spaces, while travelling or from branch offices, connected by digital tools such as Zoom, Teams and Google Drive. Option D is the opposite, option B describes outsourcing, and option C is about working hours, not location.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which is a benefit of remote work systems for the EMPLOYER?

options.d: Reduced office expenses and access to talent from a wider area

questions.explanation: Employers save on office space and running costs and can hire skilled people regardless of location. Options C, B and A are disadvantages of remote work.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: During a lockdown or public emergency, remote work systems are especially important to an organisation because they:

options.a: Allow the business to continue operating even when staff cannot come to the office
options.b: Guarantee that no cyber attacks will occur
options.c: Remove the need to set performance objectives
options.d: Eliminate the need for any communication

questions.explanation: Remote work supports business continuity: staff can keep working from wherever they are when offices are closed. Option D is wrong because remote work depends heavily on communication, option B ignores its security risks, and option C is wrong because tracking agreed objectives is a best practice for remote teams.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Anything that interferes with accurate communication between a sender and a receiver is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Noise is any interference, such as poor network, a loud environment or language differences, that distorts the message. Option A, the channel, is the medium that carries the message, not the interference. Option C, the grapevine, is the informal communication network in an organisation.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A sales manager in Ikeja sends a voice note to his team, but the network is so poor that the audio keeps breaking and some words are lost. In the communication process, the poor network is best described as:
questions.explanation: Noise is anything that interferes with accurate communication, and poor internet is a typical example. Option C, decoding, would be the team interpreting the message, which they cannot do properly because of the interference. Option D, encoding, was done by the manager when he put his ideas into words.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which statement about the 'concise' characteristic of effective communication is correct?

options.a: Conciseness only matters in oral communication, not in written reports
options.b: A concise message avoids unnecessary information but must not leave out essential information
options.c: Being concise means using technical jargon so that fewer words are needed
options.d: The shortest possible message is always the most effective message

questions.explanation: Concise communication cuts out unnecessary words, but concise does not mean incomplete, because a short message that omits essential information is ineffective. Option D ignores this warning. Option C confuses brevity with jargon, which actually makes a message less clear.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A memo inviting staff of a Yaba firm to a Monday 9 a.m. meeting reaches them on Tuesday afternoon. The memo was clear and correct. Which characteristic of effective communication did it fail?
questions.explanation: Timely communication arrives while the information is still useful, and a meeting invitation received after the meeting is useless. Option A does not apply because the memo's details were correct. Options C and B are about length and suitability of language, which were not the problem here.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A company's letter to a regulator contains correct, complete and timely information, but it is written in street slang with emojis. Which characteristic of effective communication is missing?
questions.explanation: Appropriate communication uses language, tone and a medium that suit the audience, and slang with emojis does not suit a regulator. Options B, D and A are all satisfied in the scenario, since the letter was on time, complete and correct.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Communication that follows officially recognised organisational structures and channels, is usually documented and can be traced to an identifiable source is called:
questions.explanation: Formal communication follows the official structure, for example official emails, written reports and policy documents, and it is documented and traceable. Options B and C describe the unofficial network that operates outside these structures. Option A is communication without words, such as gestures.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Information that flows from higher levels of management to lower levels, such as policies, instructions and organisational objectives, is known as:
questions.explanation: Downward communication moves from senior management to subordinates and typically carries policies, instructions and objectives. Option C flows the other way, from employees to management. Option A takes place between people at the same level.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Staff of a Lagos bottling company drop complaints and suggestions in a suggestion box that is opened weekly by the General Manager. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Upward communication flows from lower levels to management and includes complaints, suggestions, reports and feedback. Option B is the reverse direction. Option C is wrong because a suggestion box is an official channel, not the informal grapevine.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: The marketing manager of a Lagos FMCG firm meets the finance manager, who is at the same level, to agree on next quarter's advertising budget. This is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal communication occurs between employees or departments at the same organisational level, and this exact pairing is the standard example. Option C, diagonal communication, would involve people at different levels in different departments. Options A and D involve movement up or down the hierarchy.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: An HR Manager contacts a Sales Officer in another department directly, without going through the Sales Manager. This type of communication is:
questions.explanation: Diagonal communication cuts across different departments and different levels, outside the standard reporting line, and can speed up decisions. Option A needs both people to be at the same level, which is not the case here. Options D and B describe flows within one chain of command.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Rumours spreading through informal channels can harm an organisation in several ways. Which of the following is NOT one of those harmful effects?

options.c: They create a permanent official record of decisions

questions.explanation: Rumours may distort information, create anxiety, damage reputations and reduce employee trust. Creating a permanent official record is a feature of formal written communication, not of rumours. Options B, D and A are all listed harmful effects.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which pairing correctly contrasts formal and informal communication?

options.a: Formal: based on personal relationships; Informal: based on organisational objectives
options.b: Formal: written records available; Informal: usually no records
options.c: Formal: does not follow hierarchy; Informal: follows hierarchy
options.d: Formal: fast and flexible; Informal: slow and planned

questions.explanation: Formal communication is official, planned and recorded, while informal communication is unofficial and usually leaves no records. Option D reverses the speed contrast, since formal communication tends to be slower. Options C and A also swap the features of the two types.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A Lagos manufacturing company issues a press release to the media, writes to its bankers and sends an annual report to investors. These are examples of:
questions.explanation: External communication takes place between the organisation and outsiders such as customers, suppliers, banks, government, investors and the media. Option D is communication within the organisation. Option B is a type of internal communication between people at the same level.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of oral communication?

options.c: It is too slow for urgent matters
options.d: There is usually no permanent record

questions.explanation: Oral communication through meetings, phone calls and interviews gives quick, personal, immediate feedback, but it leaves no permanent record and can be misunderstood. Options A, B and C describe the opposite of oral communication's real advantages.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: In a contract dispute, a Lagos construction firm presents a signed letter in court to prove what was agreed with a supplier. Which advantage of written communication does this show?

options.a: It can serve as legal evidence
options.d: It avoids the need for a channel

questions.explanation: Written communication such as letters, reports and memos provides a permanent, accurate record that can serve as legal evidence. Options B and C are advantages of oral communication. Option D is wrong because every message needs a channel.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Facial expressions, eye contact, gestures, body language and appearance are all forms of:
questions.explanation: Non-verbal communication takes place without words, and sometimes body language says more than spoken words. Option D, visual communication, uses images and symbols such as charts, graphs and infographics. Options C and A both use words.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: An IT consultant explains a new system to market traders using terms like 'API latency' and 'cloud instances', and the traders understand very little. The main barrier here is a:
questions.explanation: Language barriers include different languages, technical jargon and poor vocabulary, and here the jargon blocks understanding. Option C covers things like noise, distance and faulty equipment. Option A covers emotions such as fear, stress and anger.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A newly employed graduate is too afraid of the Managing Director to report a costly error he noticed. Which barrier to communication does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Psychological barriers arise from the state of mind of the people communicating, such as fear, stress, anger or lack of confidence. Option A refers to structural problems like a long chain of command or information overload. Option B needs a language or jargon problem, which is not present.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A business report is best described as:

options.a: An informal verbal update given by a supervisor during a lunch break
options.b: A personal opinion piece written by an employee for social media
options.c: A short notice pinned on the staff board announcing a public holiday
options.d: A formal written document that presents facts, findings, analysis and recommendations to help management make informed decisions

questions.explanation: A business report is formal and written, and it presents facts, findings, analysis and recommendations in a structured, objective way to support decisions. Option A is informal and oral. Option B is subjective, while a good report must be objective and evidence-based.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: A supermarket chain produces a monthly sales report that simply lists sales by branch, and a separate report that explains why profits are falling and recommends solutions. These two reports are, respectively:

options.a: A progress report and a research report
options.b: An analytical report and an informational report
options.c: An informational report and an analytical report
options.d: A financial report and a progress report

questions.explanation: An informational report provides facts only, such as a monthly sales report, while an analytical report adds analysis and recommendations, such as a report on declining profits. Option B reverses the two. Option A is wrong because a progress report tracks a project and a research report presents research findings.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Every Friday, a site engineer sends management an update on how far the construction of a new warehouse in Ota has gone. This is a:
questions.explanation: A progress report shows how far a project has gone, which is exactly what a weekly construction update does. Option C presents findings from research. Option A contains financial statements such as the income statement and balance sheet.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: In the structure of a business report, the section that explains how the information in the report was gathered is the:
questions.explanation: The methodology section explains the methods used to collect and analyse information, and it comes after the introduction and objectives but before the findings. Option B gives the suggested actions. Option C holds supporting documents at the end of the report.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a good business report?
questions.explanation: A good business report is clear, accurate, concise, objective, well-organised, evidence-based and easy to understand, so a subjective report based on personal opinion fails the test. Options D, C and B are all listed qualities of a good report.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Managerial communication refers to:

options.a: The informal chats among employees during lunch and social events
options.b: Advertising messages that managers send to the firm's customers
options.c: The exchange of information between managers and employees for planning, organising, leading, controlling and decision-making
options.d: Communication that takes place only among top executives at board meetings

questions.explanation: Managerial communication is the exchange of information between managers and employees to carry out the management functions and make decisions. Option D is too narrow because it leaves out employees. Option A describes the grapevine, and option B is external marketing communication.

questions.topic: Business Communication, Information Systems and Digital Management
questions.question: Digital communication in organisations is best defined as:

options.a: The exchange of information using electronic devices and digital technologies
